name: 60/40 Portfolio (US)
author: Benchmark

source.title: Classic balanced portfolio

plain_english: 60% in US stocks (S&P 500) and 40% in 7-10 year US Treasuries, rebalanced monthly. It is the standard yardstick for a balanced investor: any tactical strategy should beat it on risk, return, or both.
rules: Hold 60% SPY and 40% IEF.
Rebalance back to 60/40 at every month-end.

name: US Stocks (S&P 500)
author: Benchmark

source.title: S&P 500 total return

plain_english: 100% in the S&P 500 with dividends reinvested. Shows what equity-market risk alone delivered.
rules: Hold 100% SPY.

name: Global 60/40
author: Benchmark

source.title: Global balanced portfolio

plain_english: A globally diversified balanced mix: 35% US stocks, 18% developed international, 7% emerging markets, and 40% US bonds. Closer to what a large pension fund's liquid public-market sleeve looks like.
rules: 35% SPY, 18% EFA, 7% EEM, 20% IEF, 20% AGG.
Rebalance monthly.

name: OTPP-shaped Reference Mix (liquid proxy)
author: Benchmark

source.title: Ontario Teachers' 2025 Annual Report - asset mix, p.32 (illustrative liquid proxy)

plain_english: An illustrative, liquid stand-in for the shape of OTPP's 2025 asset mix: 43% equity, 23% fixed income, 20% inflation-sensitive, 23% real assets, 14% credit and 9% absolute return, financed by borrowing 32% at the T-bill rate (OTPP's 'Funding and other' line). Private assets are proxied with listed ones, so this is a teaching device, not a replica of OTPP's portfolio or returns.
rules: Equity 43%: SPY 22%, EFA 14%, EEM 7%.
Fixed income 23%: IEF 12%, TLT 11%.
Inflation sensitive 20%: commodities (DBC) 10%, gold (GLD) 10%.
Real assets 23%: US REITs (VNQ) 12%, utilities as an infrastructure stand-in (XLU) 11%.
Credit 14%: investment-grade corporates (LQD).
Absolute return 9%: cash (BIL).
Funding -32%: borrow at the T-bill rate. Net cash = -23%.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Gross exposure is 132% of capital, matching the leverage implied by the 2025 report. Borrowing is charged at the T-bill rate with no spread, which flatters the proxy slightly.

name: Flexible Asset Allocation (FAA)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Hugo S. van Putten

source.title: Generalized Momentum and Flexible Asset Allocation (FAA): An Heuristic Approach

plain_english: Each month the seven asset classes are scored on three things: how much they rose over the last four months, how calm they were, and how little they moved in step with the others. The three best overall scores are bought in equal parts, but any of them that actually lost money over four months is swapped for short-term Treasuries.
rules: At the last trading day close of each month compute R, V, C for all 7 assets (the cash fund is ranked like any other asset).
Compute the rank-based loss L_i and select the 3 assets with the lowest L.
Absolute momentum: any selected asset with R_i <= 0 is replaced by the cash asset (SHY / VFISX).
Weight each of the 3 slots 1/3; cash slots add up in the cash asset.
Hold until the next month-end; rebalance the whole portfolio monthly.
notes: Paper universe (mutual funds): VTSMX (US stocks), FDIVX (foreign stocks), VEIEX (EM), VFISX (short Treasuries = cash), VBMFX (US aggregate bonds), QRAAX (commodities), VGSIX (REITs); paper sample 1998-2012 with daily data. ETF mapping above follows TuringTrader's splice choices; AllocateSmartly tracks FAA but its rules page is members-only, so its exact ETFs are not verified. Rule details were cross-checked against TuringTrader source (Keller_FAA.cs) and BestFolio/Alpha Architect summaries because the SSRN PDF was not downloadable (Cloudflare). Tie-breaking of equal L values is unspecified. Whether R<=0 or R<0 triggers replacement is not stated precisely (TuringTrader keeps an asset only if R>0). Paper also discusses rank-weighted and log-loss variants (not catalogued).

name: Elastic Asset Allocation - Golden Offensive (EAA)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Adam Butler

source.title: A Century of Generalized Momentum: From Flexible Asset Allocations (FAA) to Elastic Asset Allocation (EAA)

plain_english: Every asset gets a score that rewards strong recent gains and low correlation with the rest of the universe; the offensive version squares the return term so the leaders get much bigger weights. Money is spread over the top few scorers in proportion to their scores, and the share of the universe that is losing money is parked in Treasuries.
rules: At month-end compute r_i, v_i, c_i and z_i for every universe asset.
Crash protection: CP = (number of assets with r_i <= 0) / N; allocate CP to the cash asset (IEF).
Select the TopN assets by z_i, TopN = min(1 + ceil(sqrt(N)), floor(N/2)) = 3 for N = 7 (Kipnis' code default is 1 + ceil(sqrt(N)) = 4).
Weight selected assets w_i = (1 - CP) * z_i / sum(z_j over TopN); the cash asset can also be selected on its own score.
Hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: SSRN PDF not accessible; rules assembled from TrendXplorer's primer (co-developer blog), Kipnis' IKTrading EAA.R code, CXO and Quantopian-archive quotes of section 4.6 (excess return over 13-week T-bill). UNIVERSE IS A BEST READING: the paper used index universes of N=7, 15, 38 over 1914-2014; the CAA paper (same data set, 'Keller 2014b') lists N=8 = S&P 500, EAFE, EEM, US Tech, Japan, T-Bills, US Gov10y, US High Yield, so EAA's N=7 is assumed to be that set minus T-bills, mapped to ETFs above. AllocateSmartly tracks EAA Offensive/Defensive but rules and ETFs are members-only. Discrepancies: TrendXplorer's primer used total (not excess) returns and IEF as cash; Kipnis' prototype used the FAA mutual funds with VBMFX as cash; whether the cash asset is counted in CP is handled differently (TrendXplorer excludes it). Exact return averaging ((R1+R3+R6+R12)/22) follows Kipnis' code.

name: Elastic Asset Allocation - Golden Defensive (EAA)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Adam Butler

source.title: A Century of Generalized Momentum: From Flexible Asset Allocations (FAA) to Elastic Asset Allocation (EAA)

plain_english: Same machinery as the offensive version, but the score leans much harder on low correlation and only mildly on return, so weights are flatter and more diversified. Losing assets again push a proportional slice of the portfolio into Treasuries.
rules: At month-end compute r_i (excess 1/3/6/12-month average), v_i, c_i (12 monthly returns) and z_i.
CP = (number of assets with r_i <= 0) / N goes to the cash asset (IEF).
Select TopN = min(1 + ceil(sqrt(N)), floor(N/2)) assets by z_i (3 for N = 7).
Weight w_i = (1 - CP) * z_i / sum(z_j over TopN).
Hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: Golden Defensive exponents (wC=1, wS=0.5) come from TrendXplorer's primer and the IKTrading demo; Kipnis' first blog prototype instead suggested wS=1 for a 'defensive' setting - flagged as a discrepancy. Universe is the same best reading as eaa_golden_offensive (not verified). Paper also defines 'Equal Weighted Hedged' (wS=0, wC=1) and 'Equal Weighted Return' (wS=wC=0) variants, not catalogued separately.

name: Classical Asset Allocation - Offensive (CAA, TV=10%)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Adam Butler, Ilya Kipnis

source.title: Momentum and Markowitz: A Golden Combination

plain_english: A classic Markowitz optimiser fed only with recent data: expected returns come from 1-12 month momentum and risk from the last year of monthly returns. It picks the mix with the highest expected return for a 10% volatility budget, never putting more than a quarter in any one risky asset, and can sit fully in bonds and bills when nothing is trending.
rules: At month-end compute mu_i and the 12-month covariance matrix for all 8 assets.
Build the long-only, capped efficient frontier (CLA).
Select the efficient portfolio with annualized volatility = 10%.
Trade to those weights at the close; hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: Paper universe N=8 indices (Jan 1915-Dec 2014): S&P 500, EAFE, Emerging Markets, US Technology, Japan Topix, T-Bills, US Gov10y, US High Yield; AllocateSmartly maps these to SPY, EFA, EEM, QQQ, EWJ, BIL, IEF, HYG (EEM data before 1989 excluded by AS). Paper also has N=16 (FF sectors + bonds) and N=39 universes, not catalogued. Return estimate: the paper says equal weights on 1, 3, 6, 12-month lookbacks; AllocateSmartly (and Kipnis' code style) use sum/22, whereas TuringTrader uses (1*R1 + 3*R3 + 6*R6 + 12*R12)/22 - flagged discrepancy. Not specified in paper or AS: what to do if the target volatility is unreachable; best reading: if the maximum-return corner portfolio has vol < TV hold it, if the minimum-variance portfolio has vol > TV hold the minimum-variance portfolio.

name: Classical Asset Allocation - Defensive (CAA, TV=5%)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Adam Butler, Ilya Kipnis

source.title: Momentum and Markowitz: A Golden Combination

plain_english: The same momentum-fed optimiser as the offensive version but with half the risk budget, so it usually holds a larger share of Treasuries and bills. It aims for steadier returns with smaller drawdowns.
rules: At month-end compute mu_i = (R1+R3+R6+R12)/22 and the 12-month monthly-return covariance.
Build the long-only efficient frontier with 25% caps on risky assets and no caps on IEF/BIL.
Select the efficient portfolio with annualized volatility = 5%.
Hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: See caa_offensive for paper vs AllocateSmartly differences (return averaging, unreachable-target handling, EEM pre-1989 data).

name: Protective Asset Allocation - PAA2 (high protection, Top6, IEF)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Protective Asset Allocation (PAA): A Simple Momentum-Based Alternative for Term Deposits

plain_english: The strategy counts how many of twelve major asset classes are above their one-year average price. The fewer that are trending up, the more of the portfolio goes into intermediate Treasuries; once half or more are down it is entirely in Treasuries. The rest is split equally among the six strongest assets.
rules: At month-end compute MOM for the 12 risky assets.
Count n = assets with MOM > 0; BF = 100% if n <= 6, else BF = (12 - n)/6.
Put BF in IEF.
Put (1 - BF) equally into the TopN = 6 risky assets with the highest MOM (only those with MOM > 0; with a=2 all six are positive whenever BF < 100%).
Hold to next month-end; rebalance the full portfolio monthly.
notes: Paper universe used IYR (real estate) and GSG (commodities); AllocateSmartly uses VNQ and DBC and starts its backtest in 1989. Paper's main safe asset was IEF only (CXO summary; also BAA paper fn 3 'we focussed on PAA2 IEF'), although the paper notes SHY/IEF momentum switching could be more robust in rising-rate regimes (see paa_cpr). In-sample optimum (1971-1992): SMA12, a=2, Top6. Momentum 'bad' = non-positive.

name: Protective Asset Allocation - CPR (IEF or cash as protection)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Protective Asset Allocation (PAA): A Simple Momentum-Based Alternative for Term Deposits

plain_english: Identical to standard PAA except the safe bucket chooses between intermediate Treasuries and cash, picking whichever has been trending better. This aims to avoid holding bonds while bond prices themselves are falling.
rules: Compute MOM = P_t/SMA13 - 1 for the 12 risky assets plus IEF and cash (BIL).
n = risky assets with MOM > 0; BF = 100% if n <= 6, else (12 - n)/6.
Allocate BF to the better of IEF vs cash by MOM.
Allocate (1 - BF)/6 to each of the 6 highest-MOM risky assets.
Hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: AllocateSmartly substitutes cash (3-month UST) for the paper's SHY, citing frequent trading and low yields. Allocates ~52% to protection on average per AS.

name: Protective Asset Allocation - PAA1 (medium protection)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Protective Asset Allocation (PAA): A Simple Momentum-Based Alternative for Term Deposits

plain_english: A milder version of PAA: Treasuries are added more gradually as assets fall below trend, and the portfolio only goes fully defensive when three-quarters of the asset classes are trending down.
rules: Compute MOM = P_t/SMA13 - 1 for the 12 risky assets.
n = assets with MOM > 0; BF = min(1, (12 - n)/9) into IEF.
Split (1 - BF) equally over the top min(n, 6) risky assets by MOM (only positive-momentum assets are held; fewer are held if fewer are positive).
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Paper variant, not tracked by AllocateSmartly. Universe shown with the paper's IYR/GSG; VNQ/DBC are acceptable substitutes. Equal weight per selected asset assumed to be (1-BF)/min(n, TopN) per CXO wording ('fewer are held'); TrendXplorer notes this case is not stated explicitly - flag.

name: Protective Asset Allocation - PAA0 (low protection)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Protective Asset Allocation (PAA): A Simple Momentum-Based Alternative for Term Deposits

plain_english: The least defensive PAA setting: the Treasury share simply equals the fraction of the twelve asset classes that are below trend.
rules: Compute MOM = P_t/SMA13 - 1 for the 12 risky assets.
BF = (12 - n)/12 into IEF, n = assets with MOM > 0.
Split (1 - BF) equally over the top min(n, 6) positive-momentum risky assets.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Paper variant; per TrendXplorer it reduced volatility vs GTAA but failed the authors' absolute-return criteria. Not tracked by AllocateSmartly. Same Top-N ambiguity as paa1.

name: Generalized Protective Momentum (GPM)
author: Jan Willem Keuning, Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Generalized Protective Momentum (Seeking Alpha article)

plain_english: Like PAA, but each asset's recent return is discounted by how closely it moves with the overall basket, so diversifying assets such as gold or commodities get a boost. The three best scores are held, and the number of asset classes with negative scores decides how much is moved into Treasuries or cash.
rules: At month-end compute r_i, c_i, z_i for the 12 risky assets and for IEF and cash.
CP = 100% if n <= 6, otherwise (12 - n)/6.
CP goes to whichever of IEF and cash (SHY in the original) has the higher z.
(1 - CP) is split equally (1/3 each of the remainder) over the 3 risky assets with the highest z.
Hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: Original published by Keuning on Seeking Alpha (Aug 2016) and TrendXplorer; not an SSRN paper. Original used SHY as the short-duration alternative; AllocateSmartly substitutes cash. AS asset proxies differ slightly from the authors'. HAA paper confirms GPM uses 13612U momentum. How z is computed for the cash asset (correlation of T-bill returns with the risky EW index) follows AS wording ('the one with the higher z').

name: Vigilant Asset Allocation - G4 Aggressive (VAA-G4, T1/B1)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and Vigilant Asset Allocation (VAA): Winning More by Losing Less

plain_english: Four broad assets act as their own early-warning system: if every one of them has positive short-weighted momentum, the single strongest is bought; if even one is weakening, the whole portfolio moves into the strongest of three bond funds. It is very concentrated and switches often.
rules: At month-end compute 13612W for the 4 offensive and 3 defensive assets.
If all 4 offensive assets have positive momentum, hold 100% in the offensive asset with the highest momentum.
If any offensive asset has non-positive momentum, hold 100% in the defensive asset with the highest momentum (even if negative).
Hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: Paper's G4 universe is SPY, VEA, VWO, BND (TrendXplorer lists VOO instead of SPY); AllocateSmartly uses SPY, EFA, EEM, AGG. Paper backtests from Dec 1970 with simulated ETF data; out-of-sample Dec 1993-Dec 2016. TrendXplorer also mentions a G4 T2/B1 variant (top two at 50/50).

name: Vigilant Asset Allocation - G12 (paper, T2/B4)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and Vigilant Asset Allocation (VAA): Winning More by Losing Less

plain_english: Twelve global asset classes are monitored; each one with a negative trend shifts a quarter of the portfolio toward the best bond fund, and four or more negative trends mean fully defensive. Otherwise the two strongest assets are held.
rules: At month-end compute 13612W for the 12 risky and 3 cash assets.
Compute b and CF = min(1, floor(b*T/B)/T).
Hold the top round((1 - CF)*T) risky assets by momentum (regardless of sign), each at weight 1/T.
Put CF into the single cash asset with the highest momentum (even if negative).
Rebalance monthly.
notes: In-sample optimal parameters per CXO summary: G12 B=4/T=2; other paper universes (U15 FF sectors B3/T4, U6 FF size-value B1/T6) are not ETF-implementable and not catalogued. CXO: base CF = b/B 'rounded to multiples of 1/T'; rounding direction (floor) taken from TrendXplorer's 'easy trading' formula - flag. LQD appears in both risky and cash universes.

name: Vigilant Asset Allocation - Balanced (AllocateSmartly G12, T5/B4)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and Vigilant Asset Allocation (VAA): Winning More by Losing Less

plain_english: A more diversified VAA: up to five of twelve asset classes are held, and each additional asset class with a weak trend moves a fifth of the portfolio into the strongest bond fund.
rules: At month-end compute 13612W for the 12 risky and 3 cash assets.
Hold the top round((1 - CF)*5) risky assets, each 20%.
Put CF into the best cash asset by momentum.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: AllocateSmartly states G=12/T=5/B=4 but does not publish the ETFs or the CF rounding on the public page (refers to paper); universe shown is the paper's G12 (AS may substitute EEM/DBC). TrendXplorer lists T=2..5 with B=4 as acceptable G12 settings. Exact CF rounding (b/B vs floor to 1/T) used by AS is unverified - flag.

name: Defensive Asset Allocation - G12 (DAA, T6/B2)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and the Canary Universe: Defensive Asset Allocation (DAA)

plain_english: Instead of watching the twelve holdings themselves, DAA watches two 'canary' funds - emerging-market stocks and the US bond market. If both are healthy it holds the six strongest asset classes; one sick canary means half defensive, and two mean fully in the best bond fund.
rules: At month-end compute 13612W for risky, cash and canary assets.
Count bad canaries b among VWO and BND.
b = 0: 100% equally in the top 6 risky assets (1/6 each, momentum sign ignored).
b = 1: top 3 risky assets at 1/6 each (50%) plus 50% in the best cash asset.
b = 2: 100% in the best cash asset (highest 13612W, even if negative).
Rebalance monthly.
notes: This is the 'standard' DAA (TrendXplorer announcement, TuringTrader Keller_DAA_G12). AllocateSmartly tracks a single DAA whose rules are members-only; it is very likely DAA-G12 but this is unverified. Canary selected on 1926-1970 data; in-sample 1971-1993; out-of-sample 1994-Mar 2018. Paper says 'negative' momentum for bad canaries (TuringTrader uses mom < 0). Paper also tested U6/U15 Fama-French universes (not catalogued).

name: Defensive Asset Allocation - G6 (T6/B2)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and the Canary Universe: Defensive Asset Allocation (DAA)

plain_english: A six-asset version of DAA mixing US, developed and emerging stocks with corporate, Treasury and high-yield bonds, governed by the same two canaries.
rules: b = 0: all 6 risky assets at 1/6 each.
b = 1: top 3 risky by momentum at 1/6 each + 50% best cash asset.
b = 2: 100% best cash asset.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: LOW CONFIDENCE: parameters and universe come from TuringTrader's Keller_DAA_G6 class, whose comment reads 'instead of DAA-G4, we use DAA-G6'; the CXO summary of the paper lists only G12, U6, U15 and G4 universes, so G6 could not be verified as a paper variant. Note T = N = 6, so with b = 0 the whole risky universe is held.

name: Defensive Asset Allocation - G4 (T2/B1)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and the Canary Universe: Defensive Asset Allocation (DAA)

plain_english: The four-asset global DAA: hold the two strongest of US, developed, emerging stocks and US bonds while both canaries are healthy, and switch entirely to the best bond fund otherwise.
rules: If neither VWO nor BND has negative 13612W: hold the top 2 of SPY/VEA/VWO/BND at 50% each.
Otherwise: 100% in the best of SHY/IEF/LQD.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: G4 universe confirmed by CXO summary; T=2/B=1 taken from TuringTrader (which comments that this variant 'has subpar risk/return') - paper parameters for G4 not independently verified, flag.

name: Defensive Asset Allocation - aggressive DAA1-G4 (T4/B1)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and the Canary Universe: Defensive Asset Allocation (DAA)

plain_english: An aggressive DAA that is fully invested in an equal mix of four global assets while the canaries are healthy, and otherwise jumps to the best of short bills, intermediate Treasuries or a 2x leveraged Treasury fund.
rules: If both canaries have non-negative 13612W: hold all 4 risky assets (top 4 of 4) at 25% each.
Otherwise: 100% in the best of SHV/IEF/UST by 13612W.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Parameters and cash universe from TuringTrader Keller_DAA1_G4 (consistent with my recollection of the paper's DAA1 section, but the paper PDF itself was not accessible) - flag. Includes a leveraged ETF in the cash universe.

name: Defensive Asset Allocation - aggressive DAA1-G12 (T2/B1)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and the Canary Universe: Defensive Asset Allocation (DAA)

plain_english: Holds the two strongest of twelve global asset classes while both canaries are healthy and switches fully to the best defensive bond option at the first warning.
rules: If neither canary is bad: hold the top 2 risky assets at 50% each.
Otherwise: 100% in the best of SHV/IEF/UST.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: From TuringTrader Keller_DAA1_G12; not independently verified against the paper - flag.

name: Defensive Asset Allocation - minimal DAA1-U1 (SPY only)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Breadth Momentum and the Canary Universe: Defensive Asset Allocation (DAA)

plain_english: The simplest DAA: own the S&P 500 while emerging-market stocks and US bonds are both trending up, and otherwise move to the best-trending short, intermediate or leveraged Treasury fund.
rules: If neither VWO nor BND has negative 13612W: 100% SPY.
Otherwise: 100% in the best of SHV/IEF/UST.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: From TuringTrader Keller_DAA1_U1; not independently verified against the paper - flag. Note SPY's own momentum is not checked.

name: Lethargic Asset Allocation (LAA)
author: Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Growth-Trend Timing and 60-40 Variations: Lethargic Asset Allocation (LAA)

plain_english: Three-quarters of the portfolio is a permanent, equal mix of value stocks, gold and Treasuries. The last quarter sits in the Nasdaq-100 unless unemployment is rising and the stock market is in a downtrend at the same time, in which case it moves to short-term Treasuries.
rules: 75% is static: 25% IWD, 25% GLD, 25% IEF.
At month-end evaluate UE vs SMA12(UE) and SPX vs SMA10(SPX).
If UE > SMA12(UE) AND SPX < SMA10(SPX): the remaining 25% goes to SHY (cash); otherwise the 25% is in QQQ.
Rebalance all four sleeves back to 25% each monthly.
notes: CXO summary text and FAQ disagree on direction, but the logic and Philosophical Economics' rule are: unemployment ABOVE its 12m SMA = bearish. Publication lag: the paper's handling was not verified; TuringTrader and AllocateSmartly's GTT implementations use the prior month's UE (1-month lag) - recommended. Price series (price vs total return) for the SMA10 test unverified; TuringTrader uses ~200 trading-day SMA of $SPX. AllocateSmartly replaces IWD with SPY before 1975 and executes SHY as cash; AS also reports a variant that only rebalances on signal change or at year end. Uses revised (not real-time) unemployment data.

name: Lethargic Asset Allocation - G4 (global equity instead of QQQ)
author: Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Growth-Trend Timing and 60-40 Variations: Lethargic Asset Allocation (LAA)

plain_english: Same lazy structure as LAA, but the switchable quarter holds a world stock basket rather than the Nasdaq-100.
rules: 75% static: 25% each IWD, GLD, IEF.
Timed 25%: a constructed world-equity sleeve (SPY 50%, VEA 33.3%, VWO 16.7% of the sleeve) when risk-on, SHY when risk-off.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: LOW CONFIDENCE: taken from TuringTrader's Keller_LAA_G4 class, which cites 'Fig. 16' of the paper; not verified against the PDF.

name: Resilient Asset Allocation (RAA)
author: Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Lazy Momentum with Growth-Trend Timing: Resilient Asset Allocation (RAA)

plain_english: An all-weather style mix of tech stocks, small-cap value, gold and Treasuries that is held almost all the time. Only when unemployment is higher than a year ago and an emerging-market or bond canary is also weakening does it retreat to Treasuries alone.
rules: If UE(t-1) <= UE(t-13): risk-on.
Else compute canary 13612W; if either canary is <= 0: risk-off, otherwise risk-on.
Risk-on: 20% each in QQQ, IWN, GLD, IEF, TLT.
Risk-off: 50% IEF, 50% TLT.
Rebalance monthly to target weights.
notes: Described as a more aggressive LAA. Paper canaries VWO/BND (borrowed from DAA); AllocateSmartly uses EEM/AGG. Defensive about 15% of the time over Dec 1970-Nov 2020 per CXO. Uses revised unemployment data (look-ahead bias). Exact bad-canary threshold (< 0 vs <= 0) not verified.

name: Bold Asset Allocation - Balanced (BAA-G12/T6)
author: Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Relative and Absolute Momentum in Times of Rising/Low Yields: Bold Asset Allocation (BAA)

plain_english: Four canaries (US, developed and emerging stocks plus US bonds) decide the mode. If all four are trending up, the six assets furthest above their one-year average are held; if any canary weakens, the strategy holds the three best of a defensive list of bonds, TIPS and commodities, falling back to T-bills where those are weaker than cash.
rules: At month-end compute 13612W for the 4 canaries.
If all canaries have positive 13612W: hold the top 6 offensive assets by SMA12 momentum, 1/6 each (no absolute filter on offensive picks).
If any canary is negative: pick the top 3 defensive assets by SMA12 momentum, 1/3 each; any of the three whose SMA12 momentum is below BIL's is replaced by BIL.
Hold to next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: Paper (v0.981, 18 Jul 2022): Dec 1970-Jun 2022, defensive ~57% of months, turnover ~472%/yr. AllocateSmartly ETFs: canary SPY, EFA, EEM, AGG; offensive uses EEM for VWO; defensive uses AGG for BND; says it tracks 'version 2' of the paper (v1 had more universe overfitting) - the downloaded v0.981 matches AS's universes. Paper text says 'negative' canary momentum for bad. TuringTrader's BAA_v2 code uses BNDX as canary, which appears to be an error vs the paper's BND.

name: Bold Asset Allocation - Aggressive (BAA-G4/T1)
author: Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Relative and Absolute Momentum in Times of Rising/Low Yields: Bold Asset Allocation (BAA)

plain_english: The high-octane BAA: when all four canaries are healthy it puts everything into the strongest of Nasdaq-100, developed stocks, emerging stocks and bonds. Any canary weakness sends it to the defensive trio.
rules: If all 4 canaries have positive 13612W: 100% in the single offensive asset with the highest SMA12 momentum.
Otherwise: top 3 defensive assets by SMA12 at 1/3 each, replacing any with momentum below BIL by BIL.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Paper: QQQ substituted for SPY in the G4 offensive universe (in-sample optimal); FS Dec 1970-Jun 2022 R=21.0%, D=14.6%. AllocateSmartly ETFs: QQQ, EEM, EFA, AGG offensive; canary SPY, EFA, EEM, AGG; defensive uses AGG for BND.

name: Bold Asset Allocation - G12/T3 variant
author: Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Relative and Absolute Momentum in Times of Rising/Low Yields: Bold Asset Allocation (BAA)

plain_english: A middle ground between balanced and aggressive BAA that concentrates the offensive leg in the three strongest of twelve assets.
rules: All canaries positive (13612W): top 3 offensive by SMA12, 1/3 each.
Otherwise: top 3 defensive by SMA12, BIL replacing any weaker than BIL.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Robustness variant from section 5 / fig 15 of the paper; not tracked by AllocateSmartly.

name: Bold Asset Allocation - G4/T2 variant
author: Wouter J. Keller

source.title: Relative and Absolute Momentum in Times of Rising/Low Yields: Bold Asset Allocation (BAA)

plain_english: Aggressive BAA split across the two strongest offensive assets instead of one; the paper found it had the best Sharpe ratio of the BAA family.
rules: All canaries positive: top 2 offensive by SMA12, 50% each.
Otherwise: top 3 defensive by SMA12, BIL replacing any weaker than BIL.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Robustness variant from section 5 / fig 15 of the paper; not tracked by AllocateSmartly.

name: Hybrid Asset Allocation - Balanced (HAA-8, G8/T4)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Dual and Canary Momentum with Rising Yields/Inflation: Hybrid Asset Allocation (HAA)

plain_english: The inflation-protected Treasury fund (TIP) is the single canary: when it is falling, which tends to happen when yields or inflation expectations rise, everything goes to bills or intermediate Treasuries. Otherwise the four strongest of eight global assets are held equally, and any of them that is itself in a downtrend is swapped for the defensive asset.
rules: At month-end compute 13612U for TIP, the 8 offensive assets, BIL and IEF.
Defensive asset = whichever of BIL and IEF has the higher momentum.
If TIP momentum <= 0: 100% in the defensive asset.
Else: take the top 4 offensive assets by momentum at 25% each; any of the four with momentum <= 0 is replaced by the defensive asset.
Hold to next month-end; rebalance the whole portfolio monthly.
notes: Verified directly from the paper (v0.98, 5 Mar 2023; FS Dec 1970-Dec 2022: R=15.9%, D=9.7%, cash fraction 16.7%). AllocateSmartly uses EFA/EEM for VEA/VWO and PDBC for DBC, uses cash instead of BIL, and notes it initially sent bad offensive slots to cash before correcting to 'IEF or cash, whichever is stronger'. Pre-1997 TIPS data are simulated - treat with caution; paper substitutes IEF for TIP before end-1973.

name: Hybrid Asset Allocation - Simple (HAA-1, SPY only)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Dual and Canary Momentum with Rising Yields/Inflation: Hybrid Asset Allocation (HAA)

plain_english: Own the S&P 500 only when both stocks and inflation-protected Treasuries have positive average returns over 1-12 months; otherwise sit in whichever of intermediate Treasuries or T-bills is trending better. It trades only about twice a year on average.
rules: If TIP momentum > 0 and SPY momentum > 0: 100% SPY.
Otherwise: 100% in IEF if IEF momentum > BIL momentum, else BIL (cash).
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Paper FS Dec 1970-Dec 2022: R=12.8%, D=16.6%, ~1.8 trading months/yr. AllocateSmartly phrases the rule as 'TIP and SPY both positive', which is equivalent to the paper's Top1-of-1 with absolute momentum. AS also ran an adversarial test substituting IEF for TIP before Dec 2003. Paper footnote: HAA-2 (SPY/IEF risky, Top1) considered slightly less offensive.

name: Hybrid Asset Allocation - HAA-4 (G4/T2)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Dual and Canary Momentum with Rising Yields/Inflation: Hybrid Asset Allocation (HAA)

plain_english: A four-asset HAA (US stocks, developed stocks, real estate, Treasuries) holding the best two, governed by the TIP canary.
rules: If TIP momentum <= 0: 100% best of BIL/IEF.
Else: top 2 risky by momentum at 50% each, each replaced by best of BIL/IEF if its momentum <= 0.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Robustness variant (fig 11) from the paper; FS R=14.5%, D=13.7%. Not tracked by AllocateSmartly.

name: Hybrid Asset Allocation - HAA-12 (G12/T6)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Dual and Canary Momentum with Rising Yields/Inflation: Hybrid Asset Allocation (HAA)

plain_english: HAA applied to a twelve-asset global universe, holding the best half.
rules: If TIP momentum <= 0: 100% best of BIL/IEF.
Else: top 6 risky at 1/6 each, each replaced by best of BIL/IEF if its momentum <= 0.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Robustness variant (fig 10); FS R=15.9%, D=10.7%. Not tracked by AllocateSmartly.

name: Hybrid Asset Allocation - HAA-16 (G16/T8)
author: Wouter J. Keller, Jan Willem Keuning

source.title: Dual and Canary Momentum with Rising Yields/Inflation: Hybrid Asset Allocation (HAA)

plain_english: HAA applied to a sixteen-asset global universe, holding the best eight.
rules: If TIP momentum <= 0: 100% best of BIL/IEF.
Else: top 8 risky at 12.5% each, each replaced by best of BIL/IEF if its momentum <= 0.
Rebalance monthly.
notes: Robustness variant (fig 9); FS R=15.1%, D=13.1%. Not tracked by AllocateSmartly. The paper's fig 9 lists IDW in the dataset text but IWD in the universe; IWD (Russell 1000 Value) assumed.

name: Kipnis Defensive Adaptive Asset Allocation (KDA)
author: Ilya Kipnis

source.title: Right Now It's KDA... Asset Allocation (QuantStrat TradeR blog)

plain_english: A blend of ideas from other strategies: two canaries (emerging stocks and US bonds) set how much is invested, momentum picks up to five of ten asset classes, and a minimum-variance calculation sizes them so the mix is as calm as possible. Whatever is not invested goes to intermediate Treasuries if they are trending up, otherwise to cash.
rules: At month-end compute 13612W for the 10 risky assets, the 2 canaries and IEF.
Risky fraction = share of canaries with positive momentum: 2 -> 100%, 1 -> 50%, 0 -> 0%.
Select the top 5 risky assets by momentum and drop any with momentum <= 0.
Weight the survivors by long-only minimum variance using the blended covariance (single survivor gets 100% of the sleeve); scale the sleeve by the risky fraction.
Remainder goes to IEF if IEF momentum > 0, otherwise cash.
AllocateSmartly only: drop positions below 2% and redistribute proportionally.
Hold to next month-end.
notes: Universe borrowed from Butler/Philbrick's Adaptive Asset Allocation; canary from DAA. Kipnis used VWO/BND canaries and monthly endpoints; AllocateSmartly uses EEM/AGG and fixed 21/63/126/252-day lookbacks, plus the 2% minimum position rule. Kipnis also tested 1.5x/2x leverage when both canaries are positive (not catalogued). AS attributes about 1.4%/yr gap vs Kipnis to its 0.1% transaction-cost assumption.

name: Global Equities Momentum (GEM) - Traditional Dual Momentum (official rules)
author: Gary Antonacci

source.title: Dual Momentum Investing: An Innovative Strategy for Higher Returns with Lower Risk (McGraw-Hill book)

plain_english: If US stocks have beaten Treasury bills over the past year, own whichever of US or international stocks did better; if not, own a broad US bond fund. It usually holds a single fund for many months at a time.
rules: At month-end compute 12-month total returns of SPY, VEU (ACWI ex-US) and BIL (T-bills).
If R12(SPY) <= R12(BIL): hold 100% AGG (US aggregate bonds).
Otherwise hold 100% of whichever of SPY and VEU has the higher R12.
Hold to next month-end.
notes: Book indices: S&P 500, MSCI ACWI ex-US, Barclays US Aggregate Bond, 3-month T-bills (pre-ACWI splicing not verified). TrendXplorer notes the official rules (book p.98) apply absolute momentum to the S&P 500 first; the widely copied flowchart (p.101/112) differs (see gem_simplified). Antonacci's FAQ (quoted second-hand) names BIL (SHV when rates are near zero) for T-bills and BND/AGG for bonds. AllocateSmartly tracks 'Traditional Dual Momentum' but its rules/ETFs (likely SPY/EFA-or-ACWX/AGG/BIL) are members-only and not verified.

name: Global Equities Momentum - simplified flowchart version
author: Gary Antonacci

source.title: Dual Momentum Investing (McGraw-Hill book), simplified flowchart

plain_english: The commonly shared version of GEM: first choose the stronger of US and international stocks, then only own it if it beat T-bills over the past year, otherwise hold bonds.
rules: Pick the higher-R12 of SPY and VEU (relative momentum).
If the winner's R12 > R12(BIL): hold it; otherwise hold AGG.
Hold to next month-end.
notes: Differs from the official rule only when international stocks beat T-bills but US stocks do not; per TrendXplorer the official rule exits to bonds earlier and had better historical results with slightly more whipsaw. Included so both readings can be backtested.

name: Composite Dual Momentum
author: Gary Antonacci

source.title: Risk Premia Harvesting Through Dual Momentum

plain_english: Four independent mini dual-momentum strategies run side by side - stocks, credit, real estate and a 'crisis' pair of gold versus long Treasuries. Each picks the stronger of its two assets over the last year and only holds it if it beat T-bills; otherwise that quarter sits in cash.
rules: Split the portfolio into four fixed 25% modules: Equities (SPY vs EFA), Credit (LQD vs HYG), Real estate (VNQ vs REM), Economic stress (GLD vs TLT).
In each module pick the asset with the higher R12.
If the pick's R12 > R12(BIL), hold it with the module's 25%; otherwise that 25% goes to cash.
Modules stay at 25% (cash is not redistributed); rebalance monthly.
notes: AllocateSmartly's ETF choices 'subtly' differ from the paper's index pairs (paper used index proxies; exact series not re-verified because SSRN was blocked); AS splices REM history from two FTSE NAREIT indexes and starts tests in 1985. AS reports keeping modules fixed at 25% matters (letting cash be redistributed lowered Sharpe from 1.02 to 0.75). Antonacci himself prefers GEM.

name: Accelerating Dual Momentum (AllocateSmartly version, TLT/TIP bond switch)
author: Engineered Portfolio (Steve Hanly; Antonacci-family dual momentum)

source.title: Accelerating Dual Momentum Investing (engineeredportfolio.com)

plain_english: A faster dual-momentum switch between the S&P 500 and international small caps using 1-, 3- and 6-month returns. If neither is rising it holds whichever of long Treasuries or TIPS did better last month.
rules: At month-end compute the score for SPY and SCZ.
If the higher score is > 0, hold 100% of that equity fund.
Otherwise hold 100% of whichever of TLT and TIP had the higher 1-month return.
Hold to next month-end.
notes: AllocateSmartly added the TIP option (wary of long-duration Treasuries); the original used only long-term Treasuries (see accelerating_dual_momentum_original). AS flags ADM as the most volatile strategy it tracks. Not an Antonacci strategy per se, but derived from GEM.

name: Accelerating Dual Momentum (original Engineered Portfolio rules)
author: Engineered Portfolio (Steve Hanly)

source.title: Accelerating Dual Momentum Investing (engineeredportfolio.com)

plain_english: The original accelerating dual momentum: hold whichever of US large caps or international small caps has the stronger 1-6 month momentum, unless both are negative, in which case hold long-term Treasuries.
rules: If both equity scores are < 0: hold 100% long-term Treasuries (TLT; original VUSTX).
Otherwise hold 100% of the equity fund with the higher score.
Re-evaluate monthly.
notes: Original funds: VFINX (S&P 500), VINEX (Vanguard International Explorer, actively managed intl small cap), VUSTX (long Treasuries); SCZ is the ETF analogue. Author also showed a TIPS sub-variant (VUSTX vs VIPSX on 1-month return) which AllocateSmartly adopted. Sum vs average of returns gives identical decisions.

name: Ivy Portfolio (static 5-asset equal weight)
author: Mebane Faber & Eric Richardson

source.title: The Ivy Portfolio: How to Invest Like the Top Endowments and Avoid Bear Markets (book, Wiley)

plain_english: A simple endowment-style buy & hold portfolio: one fifth each in US stocks, foreign stocks, Treasuries, real estate and commodities. Nothing is ever timed; the only activity is periodically resetting the five slices back to 20%.
rules: Hold 20% each in US large-cap equities (SPY), developed international equities (EFA; IEFA after AS's 2025 ETF change), US 7-10y Treasuries (IEF), US REITs (VNQ) and diversified commodities (DBC; PDBC stitched on from ~Dec 2022).
No timing filter and no cash sleeve: the portfolio is always 100% invested.
At each rebalance date (close of the last trading day of the rebalance month) reset all five weights to exactly 20%; let weights drift between rebalances.
Before an asset has data, AS's convention elsewhere is to split the portfolio evenly among available assets (not stated specifically for Ivy) (uncertain).
notes: AS has no dedicated public post on its Ivy Portfolio. Evidence it is the static equal-weight version: (1) AS's 2019 public strategy-asset matrix lists Ivy with DBC, EFA, IEF, SPY, VNQ and NO cash column, whereas GTAA 5 has the same five plus Cash; (2) AS lists Ivy among its buy & hold portfolios (All-Weather, Permanent, Golden Butterfly); (3) in AS monthly performance tables, Ivy and GTAA 5 returns nearly coincide in months when GTAA 5 was likely fully invested (e.g. Oct-2017 1.35% vs 1.35%) but diverge sharply when GTAA 5 was partly in cash (e.g. Dec-2018 -4.74% vs -2.76%; Jan-2019 +6.85% vs +0.27%), i.e. Ivy has no trend filter. The book itself also presents the 10-month SMA timing overlay (that tactical version is tracked separately by AS as GTAA 5) and larger Ivy 10/Ivy 20 versions; AS appears to use only the 5-asset version. Rebalance frequency for AS's Ivy is not stated publicly (uncertain). Book ETF tickers not verified (book not accessible); AS conforms to its representative ETFs regardless.

name: Global Tactical Asset Allocation 5 (GTAA 5)
author: Mebane Faber

source.title: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation (Journal of Wealth Management 2007; SSRN working paper 2006, updated Feb 2009 and Feb 2013)

plain_english: Split the portfolio into five equal slices: US stocks, foreign stocks, Treasuries, real estate and commodities. Each month, keep a slice in its asset only if that asset is above its 10-month average price; otherwise park that slice in T-bills.
rules: Assign a fixed 20% slice to each of five assets: SPY (US equities), EFA (intl developed equities; IEFA from 2025), IEF (US 7-10y Treasuries), VNQ (US REITs), DBC (commodities; PDBC stitched on from ~Dec 2022).
At the close on the last trading day of each month compute each asset's 10-month SMA of month-end adjusted closes (current month-end included).
If an asset's month-end close is above its 10-month SMA, hold that asset at 20%; otherwise put that 20% slice in cash (T-bills, BIL).
Slices are independent: an asset's weight never depends on the others, and a failing slice is never redistributed to other assets.
Hold until the last trading day of the following month; rebalance all slices back to 20% monthly regardless of signal changes.
notes: Verified against Faber 2013 update (buy rule: monthly price > 10-month SMA; sell to cash when below; signals updated only at month-end; total-return series; cash = 90-day T-bills; equal 20% weights; FAQ: rebalanced monthly). AS confirms the 20% slices, 10-month MA, cash, and monthly full rebalance (tax-efficient TAA post) and a 1973 backtest start. Faber's original (and AS's) treatment of 'price' is the total-return/adjusted series. Equality case (close == SMA) unspecified; treat as not above. Faber also tested alternatives (10y bonds as cash, leverage) not used by AS.

name: Global Tactical Asset Allocation 13 (GTAA 13 / GTAA Moderate)
author: Mebane Faber

source.title: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation, February 2013 update (Extension 1: More Asset Classes; 'GTAA Moderate')

plain_english: A 13-slice global portfolio (stocks by style and region, several kinds of bonds, commodities, gold and real estate), each slice with a fixed weight. Every month a slice stays invested only if its asset is above its 10-month average; otherwise that slice sits in T-bills.
rules: Fixed target weights (Faber 2013): US large-cap value IWD 5%, US large-cap momentum MTUM 5%, US small-cap value IWN 5%, US small-cap momentum 5% (AS proxy: IWM per its Agg post; see notes), intl developed EFA 10%, emerging EEM 10%, US 10y Treasuries IEF 5%, intl 10y government bonds BWX 5%, US corporate bonds LQD 5%, US 30y Treasuries TLT 5%, commodities DBC 10%, gold GLD 10%, REITs VNQ 20%.
At each month-end close, for each asset: if close > 10-month SMA, hold its full target weight; otherwise move that asset's slice to cash (BIL).
No cross-sectional ranking; slices are independent and never redistributed to other assets.
Hold until the next month-end; rebalance every slice to its target weight monthly.
Apply AS 2025 ETF changes if replicating current AS: IWD->VTV, IWN->VBR, EFA->IEFA, EEM->IEMG; DBC->PDBC (stitched ~Dec 2022).
notes: Weights and asset list verified from the 2013 SSRN update (table on p.43/49: 5,5,5,5,10,10,5,5,5,5,10,10,20). AS has no public rules post for GTAA 13, but its Agg 3/6 post describes the same 13-asset universe and says the original GTAA 13 controlled how much each asset category could take (consistent with fixed weights). AS's 2019 public matrix shows GTAA 13 holding BWX, DBC, EEM, EFA, GLD, IEF, IWD, IWN, LQD, MTUM, TLT, VNQ + Cash (12 ETFs, no IWM), whereas Agg 3/6 includes IWM as the stand-in for US small-cap momentum. So the mapping of the 5% small-cap-momentum slice in AS's GTAA 13 is unverified (IWM, or folded into another ETF such as MTUM/IWN) (uncertain). The 10-month SMA is assumed to apply per asset as in GTAA 5 (paper describes the extension as the same timing model on more assets). Handling of assets before data exists (AS excludes EEM pre-1989 and BWX pre-mid-2002 in Agg) is not documented for GTAA 13 (uncertain: slice to cash vs redistributed).

name: Global Tactical Asset Allocation – Aggressive 3 (GTAA Agg 3)
author: Mebane Faber

source.title: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation, February 2013 update (Extension 3: GTAA Aggressive); ranking method from 'Relative Strength Strategies for Investing' (2010)

plain_english: Each month, rank 13 global asset classes by their average return over the last 1, 3, 6 and 12 months and put a third of the portfolio in each of the top three. Any of those three that has fallen below its 10-month average is replaced by T-bills for that third.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month compute MOM_i (simple average of 1, 3, 6 and 12-month total returns) for each of the 13 assets.
Rank assets by MOM_i descending and select the top 3 (relative momentum). Tie-break not specified (use deterministic order, e.g. higher r12).
Each selected asset gets a fixed 1/3 slice. If a selected asset's close is below its 10-month SMA, its 1/3 slice goes to cash (BIL) instead; the slice is NOT passed to the 4th-ranked asset.
Hold until the last trading day of the next month; rebalance the whole portfolio monthly.
Assets lacking history are excluded from ranking (AS: EEM excluded before 1989, BWX before mid-2002).
AS 2025 ETF changes: IWD->VTV, IWN->VBR, EFA->IEFA, EEM->IEMG; DBC->PDBC (~Dec 2022).
notes: Rules taken from the AS post and verified against Faber 2013 (top 6 or top 3 of 13 ranked on average of 1/3/6/12-month total returns; only held if above long-term MA, else that portion to cash). AS notes the absolute-momentum filter binds only ~5% of months for Agg 3. AS results are well below the paper's, which AS attributes mainly to Fama-French proxies in the original. Faber's 2010 RS paper used a 1/3/6/9/12 combination for its own tests, but the 2013 paper (and AS) use 1/3/6/12. Tie-breaking unspecified. AS live-trading nuance: signals use the closing auction print; a tiny price difference vs last real-time price once flipped an Agg 6 slice (AS 'when the close is not really the close' post).

name: Global Tactical Asset Allocation – Aggressive 6 (GTAA Agg 6)
author: Mebane Faber

source.title: A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation, February 2013 update (Extension 3: GTAA Aggressive)

plain_english: Same as the Agg 3 version, but it holds the six strongest of the 13 asset classes, one sixth each. Any of the six that is below its 10-month average is swapped for T-bills.
rules: At the month-end close compute MOM_i for the 13 assets.
Select the 6 assets with the highest MOM_i (tie-break unspecified).
Each selected asset gets a fixed 1/6 slice; if it closes below its 10-month SMA its 1/6 goes to cash (BIL), not to the 7th-ranked asset.
Hold until next month-end; rebalance the full portfolio monthly.
Exclude assets without history (AS: EEM before 1989, BWX before mid-2002); same 2025 ETF substitutions as Agg 3.
notes: Identical to Agg 3 except top_n = 6 and 1/6 slices (AS post). Faber's 2013 paper presents top-6 as the main Aggressive model and top-3 as a variant. AS: trend filter changes allocations in ~20% of months for Agg 6. AS documented a real-time vs official-close discrepancy on 11/30/2021 that moved ~17% from cash to TLT in Agg 6.

name: The Trinity Portfolio (Lite)
author: Mebane Faber (Cambria Investment Management)

source.title: The Trinity Portfolio (Cambria white paper; AS links Trinity_WP_122816_A.pdf, dated Dec 2016)

plain_english: Half the money sits permanently in a global market-style mix of stocks, bonds, commodities, gold and real estate (with value and momentum tilts). The other half is invested each month in the five strongest of those assets by recent momentum, 10% each, but only if each is above its 10-month average; otherwise that 10% sits in T-bills.
rules: Static half (50% of portfolio, % of TOTAL portfolio): MTUM 4.50, IWD 4.50, EFV 6.75, EEM 2.25, LQD 9.90, TLT 6.75, BWX 7.20, TIP 0.90, DBC 2.50, GLD 2.50, VNQ 2.25 (sums to 50%).

Dynamic half (50%): at the month-end close score each of 10 entities by the average of 1, 3, 6 and 12-month total return; MTUM and IWD are treated as ONE US-equity entity (always selected/filtered together).

Select the top 5 entities (top half). Each gets a fixed 10% slice (one fifth of the dynamic half) if its close is above its 10-month SMA; otherwise that 10% goes to cash (BIL). A US-equity selection is split between MTUM and IWD (presumably 5%/5%) (uncertain).
AS 2% minimum-position rule: when TIP is not selected by the dynamic half, its 0.9% static allocation is moved to TLT (so TLT static becomes 7.65%).
Final weight per ETF = static weight + any dynamic slice; hold until the next month-end; rebalance monthly.
Current AS tickers: EEM->IEMG and IWD->VTV after 2025 changes; DBC->PDBC (~Dec 2022).
notes: Static weights read from the allocation image in the AS post ('Trinity Permanent Allocation'). AS calls it 'Lite' because it replaces the white paper's individual-stock factor exposures (US momentum/value, intl value) with MTUM/IWD/EFV and Faber's sovereign-bond selection with BWX, and expands 10 asset classes to 11 ETFs. Original Cambria white paper could not be retrieved (links 404) so the paper's own weights/versions (e.g., different static/dynamic splits) are unverified. Ambiguities: how the MTUM+IWD composite momentum/SMA is computed (AS offers the math on request only); whether TIP's 0.9% also moves to TLT when TIP is selected but fails its SMA (likely, since the rule is about sub-2% positions) (uncertain); tie-breaks unspecified.

name: 12-Month High Switch [Dynamic Bond]
author: Mebane Faber

source.title: 12-Month High Switch Model (Meb Faber; AS does not cite the specific publication)

plain_english: Five assets (US stocks, foreign stocks, real estate, gold, commodities) each get 20% only when they are trading within 5% of their highest month-end price of the past year. Money not used goes to intermediate Treasuries, but only if Treasuries are also near their 12-month high; otherwise it waits in T-bills.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month compute H12 for SPY, EFA (IEFA from 2025), VNQ, GLD and commodities (DBC, PDBC from ~Dec 2022).
Allocate a fixed 20% to each of these five assets whose month-end close is within 5% of its 12-month high.

Pool the unallocated 20% slices into the defensive sleeve. AS-tracked Dynamic Bond version: put the pool in IEF only if IEF is itself within 5% of its own 12-month high; otherwise put the pool in cash (BIL).
Original (non-tracked) version: unallocated slices always go to IEF.
Hold until the next month-end; rebalance monthly.
Before an asset has sufficient history, split the portfolio evenly among the remaining assets (AS calc note; commodities data from 12/1969, VNQ proxy from 12/1971).
notes: AS tracks ONLY the Dynamic Bond variant on its platform (stated in AS post). Original Faber publication not identified/verified (AS links mebfaber.com, SSRN 962461 and cambriafunds.com/insights generically). 'Within 5%' interpreted as P >= 0.95*H12; equality and whether the high uses closes only (yes, month-end closes per AS) are as stated by AS. AS lists commodities as PDBC in this 2024 post (DBC stitched to PDBC).

name: Sector Relative Strength
author: Mebane Faber

source.title: Relative Strength Strategies for Investing (Cambria working paper, April 2010)

plain_english: Each month, buy the US stock-market sectors that have risen the most over the past year (blending several look-back periods) and hold them equally. When the overall market is in a downtrend (below its 10-month average) the strategy steps aside into T-bills.
rules: At the month-end close rank the US sector ETFs by MOM_i (trailing total-return momentum).
Select the top 3 sectors and weight them equally (1/3 each) (uncertain: paper reports Top 1, Top 2 and Top 3 variants; AS's choice not public).

Dynamic hedge (paper's version): if the S&P 500 closes below its 10-month SMA, move the entire portfolio to cash (T-bills/BIL) (uncertain whether AS uses this market-level filter or a per-sector 10-month SMA filter; the paper says both give similar results).
A sector that drops out of the top N is sold at the monthly rebalance and replaced by the new top-N member.
Hold until the next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: LOW CONFIDENCE ON AS SPECIFICS. AS has no public rules post for this strategy (the AS 'Sector Rotation with Fama-French Alphas' post is an unrelated, rejected strategy). AS's 2019 matrix confirms only that it trades 'US Sectors (Multiple)' plus Cash. Rules above follow Faber's 2010 paper (verified): rank 10 sectors on trailing total returns over 1-12 months or the average of 1/3/6/9/12; hold top 1/2/3 equally; optional dynamic hedge to 100% T-bills when S&P 500 < 10-month SMA (or per sector). AS's exact sector list, lookback combination, number held and filter design are NOT verified. Faber also suggests a sell filter (buy top 3, sell when out of top 5) to cut turnover; not known to be used by AS.

name: Tactical Yield
author: Mebane Faber

source.title: T-Bills and Chill...Most of the Time (Cambria Investments white paper, Feb 2025)

plain_english: Own intermediate Treasuries only when they pay unusually well over T-bills, and own corporate bonds only when their yield over T-bills is unusually high, judged against all past history. Otherwise sit in T-bills.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month compute the term premium (10-year Treasury yield minus 3-month T-bill yield) and the credit premium (investment-grade corporate bond yield minus 3-month T-bill yield).
Compare each premium with its own full history up to that date (no look-ahead).
If the term premium is in the top half of its history, allocate 50% to IEF; otherwise that 50% stays in cash (BIL).
If the credit premium is in the top half of its history, allocate 50% to LQD; otherwise that 50% stays in cash.
Hold until the next month-end; rebalance monthly.
notes: Rules from the AS post (2026). Original Cambria PDF link returned 404, so the exact yield series (especially which IG corporate yield), whether yields are month-end or monthly averages, and whether 'top half' is > or >= median could not be verified (uncertain). No publication-lag issue for market yields if month-end daily yields are used; if monthly-average series are used, they are only known after month-end (AS approach not stated). AS notes small early-history discrepancies vs Faber (~1932) due to data sources. AS tested cutoffs 30-70%; 50% is the tracked setting.

name: Robust Asset Allocation – Balanced (RAA Balanced)
author: Wesley Gray (Alpha Architect), with Jack Vogel and David Foulke

source.title: DIY Financial Advisor: A Simple Solution to Build and Protect Your Wealth (Wiley); Alpha Architect 'Robust Asset Allocation' blog posts

plain_english: A diversified mix of US and foreign stocks (tilted to value and momentum), real estate, commodities and a large slice of Treasuries. Each slice is cut in half when one of two simple 12-month trend tests fails and moved fully to T-bills when both fail.
rules: Target weights (uncertain, not verified from source): US equity 20% split value IWD 10% / momentum MTUM 10%; international equity 20% split value EFV 10% / EFA 10% (stand-in for intl momentum); US REITs VNQ 10%; commodities DBC 10%; 7-10y Treasuries IEF 40%.
At each month-end compute the two trend rules per asset: price above its 12-month SMA, and 12-month total return above the T-bill return over the same 12 months.
Hold target_weight x 1.0 if both rules are positive, x 0.5 if exactly one is positive, x 0 if neither (uncertain); the de-risked portion goes to cash (BIL).
Trend rules assumed to apply to every sleeve including IEF (uncertain).
Hold until next month-end; rebalance all sleeves monthly.
AS 2025 ETF changes: IWD->VTV, EFA->IEFA; DBC->PDBC (~Dec 2022).
notes: LOW CONFIDENCE ON WEIGHTS. No AS public rules post exists and alphaarchitect.com returned HTTP 403, so rules are from AS mentions plus unverified recollection of the source. Verified from AS: tracked in Balanced and Aggressive versions; fixed position sizes independent of other assets and no cross-sectional momentum (AS taxes post); uses a 12-month measure, longer than GTAA's 10-month (AS posts); AS 2019 matrix universe = DBC, EFA, EFV, IEF, IWD, MTUM, VNQ + Cash for both versions. NOT verified: exact sleeve weights, the 50/50 MA+TMOM combination, whether IEF is trend-filtered, and how intl momentum maps to EFA. Verify against DIY Financial Advisor (Gray, Vogel, Foulke 2015) before use.

name: Robust Asset Allocation – Aggressive (RAA Aggressive)
author: Wesley Gray (Alpha Architect), with Jack Vogel and David Foulke

source.title: DIY Financial Advisor: A Simple Solution to Build and Protect Your Wealth (Wiley); Alpha Architect 'Robust Asset Allocation' blog posts

plain_english: The same trend-protected value/momentum asset mix as RAA Balanced, but with more in stocks and less in Treasuries. Each slice is halved or moved to T-bills when its 12-month trend tests fail.
rules: Target weights (uncertain, not verified): higher equity/real-asset share and smaller Treasury sleeve than Balanced; best recollection US equity 30% (IWD 15% / MTUM 15%), intl equity 30% (EFV 15% / EFA 15%), VNQ 10%, DBC 10%, IEF 20%.
Apply the same per-sleeve trend rules as Balanced: 100% of target if both 12-month MA and 12-month TMOM are positive, 50% if one, 0% if none; remainder to cash (BIL) (uncertain).
Hold until next month-end; rebalance monthly.
Same AS 2025 ETF substitutions as Balanced.
notes: LOW CONFIDENCE ON WEIGHTS (see RAA Balanced notes). AS's 2019 matrix shows the Aggressive version uses the same seven ETFs as Balanced including IEF, so it has a nonzero Treasury sleeve; the exact split could not be verified (alphaarchitect.com blocked, no AS public post, web search budget exhausted). Alpha Architect also published an RAA Moderate version that AS does not track. Verify weights and the signal-combination rule against DIY Financial Advisor before relying on this entry.

name: Adaptive Asset Allocation
author: Adam Butler, Michael Philbrick, Rodrigo Gordillo (GestaltU / ReSolve Asset Management)

source.title: Adaptive Asset Allocation: A Primer

plain_english: Each month, buy the half of a 10-asset global menu (stocks, REITs, Treasuries, commodities, gold) that has risen the most over the past six months. Instead of splitting money equally, size the positions to make the combined portfolio as low-volatility as possible, using recent volatility and correlation.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month compute MOM_i for all 10 assets.
Rank by MOM_i and select the top 5 (the top half of the universe). No absolute-momentum filter: the 5 are held even if their momentum is negative; there is no cash.
Before RWX data exist (AS: until mid-1999) the universe is 9 assets and the top 4 are selected (keeps the top-half rule).
Build Sigma = D*C126*D for the selected assets (20-day volatility, 126-day correlation).
Solve the long-only minimum-variance portfolio: minimise w' Sigma w subject to sum(w) = 1 and w_i >= 0.
AS practical filter: any weight below 2% of the portfolio is set to zero and its weight is redistributed proportionally to the remaining positions.
Trade at the same close; hold until the last trading day of the following month.
notes: AS says complete rules are not stated precisely in the primer; the tested rules were worked out with the authors. CSS Analytics' 2012 replication used ~6-month ROC, top 50% of assets, monthly rebalance and a short (~20-day) volatility lookback, but a reply also mentions a 60-day variance window (conflict unresolved there); AS's 20-day vol / 126-day correlation is the spec to follow. AS post text names EZU for Europe while AS's 2019 asset matrix shows VGK - verify which ETF AS currently uses. The 2% minimum-position rule is an AS addition (negligible effect). Solver/constraints beyond long-only and fully invested are not stated (AS never uses leverage/shorts). No tie-break rule given. AS conforms to standard ETFs and changed EEM->IEMG and RWX->VNQI in 2025. Not verified against the primer PDF itself (SSRN returned 403).

name: Tactical Permanent Portfolio
author: Adam Butler (GestaltU / ReSolve Asset Management)

source.title: Permanent Portfolio Shakedown Part II (GestaltU)

plain_english: Start from Harry Browne's Permanent Portfolio idea (stocks, Treasuries, gold, cash) but only hold the assets currently in an uptrend, give the calmer assets bigger weights, and move part of the portfolio to cash whenever the expected portfolio volatility would exceed 7% a year.
rules: On the trading day before the last trading day of the month (T-1), keep those of SPY, IEF and GLD whose close is above their 200-day simple moving average.
Weight the kept assets by simple inverse volatility: w_i = (1/sigma_i) / sum_j(1/sigma_j), sigma from 21-day daily returns as of T-1.
Compute the annualised volatility of this risk-parity portfolio from the 60-day covariance matrix as of T-1.
If portfolio volatility > 7%, scale all weights by 7%/vol and put the remainder in cash. If <= 7%, keep weights summing to 100% (AS uses no leverage).
If no asset is above its 200-day SMA, hold 100% cash.
Execute at the close of the last trading day of the month (T); hold until the last trading day of the next month.
notes: The linked GestaltU article only partially specifies a tactical version (it discusses a 10-month MA filter, risk-parity weighting, a 7% (and 5%) volatility target, mostly quarterly rebalancing for the base tests); the precise rules here (200-day SMA, 21-day vol, 60-day covariance, 1-day lag, monthly) come from AS's post and were not verifiable in the original. Annualisation factor (252) and whether the 60-day covariance is sample covariance of simple daily returns are assumptions. Cash is AS's cash (3-month T-bill return). AS shows IEF in this strategy although Browne's buy-and-hold PP that AS tracks uses TLT.

name: Minimum Correlation Portfolio
author: David Varadi (CSS Analytics), with Michael Kapler, Henry Bee, Corey Rittenhouse

source.title: The Minimum Correlation Algorithm: A Practical Diversification Tool

plain_english: Hold all eight major ETFs all the time, but give more money to the assets that are least correlated with the rest and less volatile, so the portfolio is spread across genuinely different return streams. Weights are recalculated each month from recent daily price behaviour.
rules: At the month-end close take the last L daily dividend-adjusted returns of the 8 ETFs.
Compute the correlation matrix and each asset's volatility.
Transform correlations into the 'adjusted' matrix A_ij = 1 - NormCDF(rho_ij, mean, sd of all off-diagonal correlations).
Average each row of A (excluding the diagonal), rank the averages so that the most-correlated asset gets the largest rank, and convert ranks to rank weights q = r/sum(r).
Multiply rank weights by A (q' A), normalise to sum to 1, divide by each asset's volatility and renormalise to 100%.
Long-only, always fully invested in all 8 assets; no trend filter, no cash. (Special cases in reference code: 1 asset -> 100%; 2 assets -> inverse volatility.)
Trade at the close and hold until the next month-end.
notes: No dedicated public AS post; AS's members page slug is 'david-varadis-minimum-correlation-portfolio' (not accessed). Universe taken from AS's public 2019 strategy/asset matrix (EEM, EFA, GLD, IWM, QQQ, SPY, TLT, VNQ), which matches the paper's 8-ETF test universe with IYR->VNQ. Algorithm steps taken from Systematic Investor's SIT R code (co-author Kapler: min.corr), as the paper PDF could not be retrieved. Paper backtest: weekly rebalance, 60-day lookback (SIT defaults). AS lookback, variant and pre-ETF data not public - flagged. AS separately tracks 'US Min Correlation' (SPY/IEF/LQD/VNQ, 36 month-end inputs) - see as_us_min_correlation; do not confuse the two.

name: Percentile Channels
author: David Varadi (CSS Analytics)

source.title: A Simple Tactical Asset Allocation Portfolio with Percentile Channels (for Dummies)

plain_english: Four asset classes are each judged on four time frames: an asset turns 'on' when its price breaks into the top quarter of its recent range and only turns 'off' when it falls into the bottom quarter. Assets that are on more often get more money, scaled down for volatility, and whatever is left over sits in cash.
rules: Track the 16 asset/lookback channel states daily (entry above the 75th percentile, exit below the 25th percentile).
At the month-end close compute Score_i = average of the 4 states (values -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1).
Compute C_i = Score_i / sigma_i (20-day volatility).
Compute W_i = |C_i| / sum_j |C_j|, where the denominator includes assets with negative scores.
Set W_i = 0 for assets with negative (or zero) score; the strategy is long-only.
Cash = 1 - sum(W_i).
Trade at the close; hold until the next month-end.
notes: Weighting formula verified from AS's public worked-example image (20-day volatility, score/vol, abs-sum normalisation including negatives, negatives ignored, cash residual), which matches Kipnis' and Systematic Investor's replications. AS text says channels are calculated at month-end; Systematic Investor and Kipnis' later update track channel crossings daily and sample at month-end - daily state tracking assumed (uncertain whether AS only checks month-end closes). Varadi's original used VTI/ICF and SHY for cash; AS conforms to SPY/VNQ and its standard cash. Percentile interpolation method not stated.

name: Growth and Inflation Sector Timing
author: David Varadi (CSS Analytics)

source.title: The Growth and Inflation Sector Timing Model

plain_english: The S&P 500's trend says whether growth is rising, and the relative performance of inflation-sensitive sectors (energy, industrials, financials, materials) versus defensive ones (utilities, health care, staples) says whether inflation expectations are rising. The strategy holds the single sector ETF that has historically done best in the resulting regime.
rules: At each daily close compute GROWTH_UP and INFLATION_UP.
Goldilocks (growth up, inflation down): 100% XLK.
Reflation (growth up, inflation up): 100% XLE.
Stagflation (growth down, inflation up): 100% XLV.
Deflation/disinflation (growth down, inflation down): 100% XLP.
Always fully invested in exactly one sector ETF; trade at the close when the regime changes, otherwise hold.
AS-tracked version adds smoothing/turnover reduction agreed with Varadi; the mechanism is not public, so a replication of the original rules will trade more often than AS's version.
notes: Regime-to-ETF map and basket weights verified from AS's public figures (pie charts 50/17/17/16 and 33/33/34; quadrant: XLE/XLV/XLK/XLP). Varadi's text also remarks that holding Staples in both down-growth regimes would be a simple option, but his explicit choice (and AS's figure) is Health Care for stagflation. Varadi confirmed the ratio uses total-return series; basket construction (daily-rebalanced fixed weights vs buy-and-hold from the start date) and the base date of the ratio are not specified - the 200-day median comparison makes the level irrelevant but the drift method matters slightly. Communication Services excluded for lack of history. Original post gives no explicit execution frequency (daily implied); AS states daily evaluation with turnover reduction (smoothing details undisclosed). Extremely concentrated single-sector strategy. Lab implementation: Original rules switch on any day the regime changes; here the regime is evaluated at month-end only (monthly approximation). The turnover-reduction AllocateSmartly agreed with the author is not public.

name: Inflation Compass - Original
author: David Varadi (CSS Analytics)

source.title: The Inflation Compass Model

plain_english: Like Growth and Inflation Sector Timing, but inflation is read directly from the bond market: inflation counts as 'on' only when 5-year breakeven inflation is above 2% and either the breakeven rate or the inflation-sensitive sectors are trending up. Each month it holds energy, tech, utilities, or a staples/Treasury mix depending on the growth/inflation regime.
rules: At the month-end close compute GROWTH_UP and INFLATION_ON.
Growth up + inflation on (reflation): 100% XLE.
Growth up + inflation off (goldilocks): 100% XLK.
Growth down + inflation on (stagflation): 100% XLU.
Growth down + inflation off (disinflationary slowdown): 50% XLP + 50% IEF.
Trade at the close; hold until the next month-end.
notes: Rules verified against Varadi's post and AS's public regime figure (XLE / XLK / XLU / XLP+IEF). Whether the regression is on the raw or log ratio is not stated; basket rebalancing method not stated. T5YIE starts 2003, yet AS's backtest starts 1990 and AS calls pre-2003 data out-of-sample - AS's pre-2003 inflation-expectation proxy is undisclosed. AS also showed robustness runs replacing T5YIE with 5y inflation swaps (USSWIT5) and Cleveland Fed EXPINF5YR (not part of the tracked rules). Varadi's own tests included a 1-day execution delay sensitivity; AS uses month-end close execution. Highly concentrated strategy.

name: Inflation Compass - Enhanced
author: David Varadi (CSS Analytics)

source.title: The Inflation Compass Model (enhancements proposed by the author to AllocateSmartly)

plain_english: The same inflation/growth compass as the Original, but instead of betting on one exact set of settings it averages the signal over many reasonable settings, which usually leaves the portfolio split between a few holdings. It also uses the Nasdaq-100 instead of the tech sector and pairs utilities with commodities in stagflation.
rules: For each parameter combination in the ensemble, determine the growth/inflation regime exactly as in the Original.
Map each regime to Enhanced holdings: reflation -> XLE; goldilocks -> QQQ (instead of XLK); stagflation -> 50% XLU + 50% PDBC; disinflation -> 50% XLP + 50% IEF.
Average the resulting allocations across all parameter combinations to get fractional weights (averaging method assumed - uncertain).
Trade at the month-end close; hold for the following month.
notes: AS describes the Enhanced version only as several author-proposed refinements, chiefly parameter ensembling; specific values not published. The QQQ-for-XLK swap and the 50/50 XLU/PDBC stagflation sleeve come from a reader comment on Varadi's post (Aug 2026) comparing AS's two versions, which Varadi's reply confirmed; other refinements, if any, are unknown. Treat this entry as a best-effort approximation; replication will not match AS exactly.

name: Macro-support softmax, US-investable 4 risky classes + cash (faithful US replication)
author: Replication of Brine, Cereda & Sueppel (2026) with US public data

source.title: Wealth management with macro factors

plain_english: A five-bucket portfolio (US stocks, 5-year Treasuries, investment-grade corporates, gold, cash). Each quarter, each bucket gets an economic support score built from growth, labour, inflation, money and real-rate data. The scores turn into weights through an exponential rule: well-supported assets get more, poorly supported ones get less, and cash is the neutral fallback.
rules: At each month-end t, build US factors from data published by t: either ALFRED as-of values, or Norgate/FRED latest values shifted by the publication lag (monthly: CPI, payrolls, UNRATE, IP, ISM, M2, CFNAI, MICH lag 1 month; real PCE, Case-Shiller, inventories/sales lag 2 months; GDP from the end of the 2nd month after quarter end; daily market data T-1).

Factors: GROWTH_NOW = 3mma CFNAI; XIP = 3mma yoy(INDPRO) - TREND (TREND = 20-quarter median of yoy real GDP); XRPCONS = 3mma yoy(real PCE) - TREND; LABTIGHT = 0.5 z(XEMPL) - 0.25 z(dUNRATE 12m) - 0.25 z(UNRATE - 60m mean); XCPI = mean(yoy and 6m/6m saar of headline and core CPI) - 2.0; XHH = MICH - 120m median; XHPI = 3mma yoy(Case-Shiller national) - 2.0; RIRY = mean(3m bill - EXPINF1YR, 5y CMT - EXPINF5YR); TP5 = Kim-Wright 5y term premium; XMON = yoy(M2) - 2.0 - TREND; MFG = ISM-50 level and 3m change; INV_CHG = 3m change of mfg inventories/sales; CONSTR_CHG = 3m % change of 3mma permits; CRCARRY = mean z(Baa-10y, CCC OAS); EQCARRY = (100/CAPE - real short rate) * 10/vol63d - 3.
Score each factor with zn; combine into themes with the stated weights; re-score multi-factor themes; average the signed themes per asset; re-score.
Weights w_i = exp(S_i) / sum_j exp(S_j) over {EQ, UST, CR, GLD, CASH} with S_CASH = 0, temperature 1, no caps.
Rebalance at quarter-end with a 1-day slip; report the faithful constant-weight PnL and the drifting buy-and-hold PnL; costs 0/5/20 bp per side.
notes: Faithful to the post's maths (scoring, conceptual parity, softmax with temperature 1, quarterly rebalance, 1-day lag). It covers only the 4 of 11 classes whose drivers are US data. US proxies stand in for global themes. Neutral-zero carry and real-rate themes give structural tilts towards credit and Treasuries. Do not expect to match the post's 8.9% vs 4.8%. Lab implementation: Lab replication with US public data. One deliberate change: excess industrial-production growth is measured against its own 5-year trend rather than trend GDP growth, because US factory output structurally grows slower than GDP and the original definition biases the US growth score downward. Labour-force growth is proxied by the 60-month median of payroll growth, building permits by housing starts, and the equity-carry leg of the gold score is omitted (no live earnings data). ISM data in Norgate stops in Aug 2026 and is carried forward. Signals at quarter-end are traded at the same close (the original trades one day later).
macro_inputs: FRED: MICH, EXPINF1YR, EXPINF5YR, THREEFYTP5, MNFCTRIRSA

name: Macro-factor tilted balanced portfolio (60/40 anchored softmax with cash anchor)
author: Tiago Costa, adapting Brine, Cereda & Sueppel (Macrosynergy, 2026)

source.title: Wealth management with macro factors

plain_english: Start from a 60/40 stock/bond mix with a little cash. When the economy looks good for stocks (solid growth, spare capacity in the labour market, contained inflation, easy money), tilt towards stocks. When it looks good for bonds (high real yields and term premia, low inflation, a weak cycle), tilt towards bonds. When neither looks good, cash grows. Example: a stock score of +1 with a neutral bond score gives about 76/19/5.
rules: Compute S_SPY and S_IEF at month-end as in ms_wm_us5_softmax, with publication lags applied.

Weights w_i = b_i * exp(S_i / tau) / sum_j b_j * exp(S_j / tau), with b = (0.54, 0.36, 0.10) and tau = 1. This is equivalent to a softmax with logits S_i + ln(b_i); equal b recovers the original formula.
Optional policy bounds: SPY 30-80%, IEF 10-60%, cash 0-40%. Clip, then move any excess or shortfall to or from cash and renormalise.
Trade at the next day's close after the quarter-end signal; costs 5 bp per side.
notes: The anchoring and the 10% cash anchor are our design choices so the post's 'cash as default' logic fits a balanced policy. The scoring and exponential weighting are faithful to the post. Unbounded with tau = 1 at the +/-3 winsor limits, the weights can become extreme, so test the bounded version too. Lab implementation: Lab replication with US public data. One deliberate change: excess industrial-production growth is measured against its own 5-year trend rather than trend GDP growth, because US factory output structurally grows slower than GDP and the original definition biases the US growth score downward. Labour-force growth is proxied by the 60-month median of payroll growth, building permits by housing starts, and the equity-carry leg of the gold score is omitted (no live earnings data). ISM data in Norgate stops in Aug 2026 and is carried forward. Signals at quarter-end are traded at the same close (the original trades one day later).
macro_inputs: FRED: MICH, EXPINF1YR, EXPINF5YR, THREEFYTP5, MNFCTRIRSA

name: Growth/inflation quadrant allocation (illustrative)
author: Tiago Costa, after Ilmanen, Maloney & Ross (2014) and Neville et al. (2021)

source.title: The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times (regime evidence); concept also in Ilmanen, Maloney & Ross (2014), 'Exploring Macroeconomic Sensitivities', JPM [citation from memory]

plain_english: Classify the economy into one of four regimes: is growth above or below trend, and is inflation above or below target? Hold the mix of stocks, bonds, inflation-linked bonds, commodities and gold that historically suits that regime.
rules: G+ I-: SPY 70, IEF 30
G+ I+: SPY 50, DBC 20, TIP 15, GLD 15
G- I+: SPY 20, TIP 30, GLD 25, BIL 25
G- I-: SPY 20, IEF 60, GLD 20
Switch quadrant only when the new quadrant holds at two consecutive month-ends; trade the next day.
notes: The quadrant weights are illustrative and not taken from any paper. The Ilmanen-Maloney-Ross citation is from memory and its regime definitions were not re-verified. The Man summary of Neville et al. reports that in US inflation regimes equities returned -7%, 10y Treasuries -5% and commodities +14% real annualised. History starts with DBC (2006) and TIP (2003); use index back-fills before that. Lab implementation: Lab replication with US public data. One deliberate change: excess industrial-production growth is measured against its own 5-year trend rather than trend GDP growth, because US factory output structurally grows slower than GDP and the original definition biases the US growth score downward. Labour-force growth is proxied by the 60-month median of payroll growth, building permits by housing starts, and the equity-carry leg of the gold score is omitted (no live earnings data).
