ISM data in Norgate stops in Aug 2026 and is carried forward. Signals at quarter-end are traded at the same close (the original trades one day later).
macro_inputs: FRED: MICH, EXPINF1YR, EXPINF5YR, THREEFYTP5, MNFCTRIRSA

name: Inflation-surge defensive overlay on 60/40
author: Tiago Costa, after Neville, Draaisma, Funnell, Harvey & Van Hemert (2021)

source.title: The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times (SSRN 3813202; Man Institute summary 'When inflation hits')

plain_english: Run a normal 60/40 portfolio. When inflation is clearly surging, swap the nominal bonds for inflation-linked bonds, commodities and gold, and only keep stocks while they are in an uptrend.
rules: OFF: hold 60/40 SPY/IEF.
ON: replace the 40% bond sleeve with 1/3 TIP, 1/3 commodities, 1/3 GLD; hold the 60% equity sleeve in SPY only if SPY >= its 10-month moving average, otherwise in BIL.
Evaluate at month-end; trade the next day.
notes: The paper defines regimes after the fact: year-on-year inflation rising well beyond 2% to 5% or more, 8 US episodes since 1926. Per the Man summary, real annualised returns in those regimes were equities -7%, 10y Treasuries -5%, 60/40 -6%, commodities +14%, and active trend-following about +25%. The 4%/3% trigger is our real-time proxy, not from the paper; the journal of publication is unverified. Few episodes after 2000 (2021-22), so the backtest evidence is thin.

name: Momentum Turning Points
author: Ashish Garg, Christian L. Goulding, Campbell R. Harvey, Michele G. Mazzoleni

source.title: Momentum Turning Points (JFE 2023; SSRN 2019) and Breaking Bad Trends (FAJ 2023)

plain_english: Classifies each asset as in a bull, bear, correction or rebound by comparing its 12-month and 2-month trends. In bulls it is fully invested, in bears it is out, and in corrections/rebounds it takes a partial position whose size is learned from how those states played out historically.
rules: For each asset, build monthly excess returns over T-bills from the earliest available data (AS: from 1958-12 for Portfolio where possible; 1926-07 French data for Simple).

Every 5 years, re-estimate a_Co and a_Re per asset from all history up to the prior month (expanding window) using the formulas in 'signal'; clip to [0,1]. (Paper: at least 12 months in each state required; BBT paper re-estimates every 30 months.)
At each month-end classify each asset's state from its 12-month and fast-window average excess returns and compute its position (+1, -1, 1-2a_Co or 2a_Re-1).
Long-only AS adaptation: negative positions are held as cash; positive position p in [0,1] scales the asset's slot.

Portfolio flavor: each of the 6 assets gets an equal slot of 1/6 (paper equal-weights within and across asset classes) times its position; unallocated remainder in cash; any final position below 2% is moved to cash.
Simple flavor: SPY only, fast window = 1 month, slot = 100%.
Hold until next month-end.
notes: AS tracks one strategy named 'Momentum Turning Points' but describes two flavors (Simple: SPY only; Portfolio: 6 assets, 2-month fast signal); which flavor is the tracked one is not stated publicly (Portfolio assumed as primary). Formulas verified from the JFE paper (Proposition 9, eq. 32-33) and the BBT paper Appendix C. AS's handling of short positions (cash vs other) and the per-asset slot weighting are not stated - long-only, no leverage, flagged as assumptions. AS notes its summary stats use normal compounded returns; only the signals use averaged monthly returns. Lab implementation: Speeds are re-estimated every 5 years on each asset's own history available in the lab (from 1988-1991 for most assets); with too little history the neutral speed 0.5 is used.

name: Predicting Bond Returns
author: Guido Baltussen, Martin Martens, Olaf Penninga

source.title: Predicting Bond Returns: 70 Years of International Evidence (Financial Analysts Journal)

plain_english: Scales exposure to intermediate Treasuries between 0% and 100% using four votes: a steep yield curve, positive bond trend, weak stocks, and weak commodities are all bullish for bonds. The rest is held in cash.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of each month compute the four component signals.
Average them (pre-1970 AS ignores the commodity component and averages the remaining three).
Allocate FINAL (0-100%) to IEF; the remainder sits in cash earning the 3-month T-bill return.
Hold until the end of the following month.
notes: AS applies the ensemble only to US Treasuries (IEF) rather than the authors' international basket. Whether the 10-year z-score window is rolling (assumed) or expanding with a 10y minimum, and whether it includes the current observation, is not stated by AS (paper not accessed: SSRN 403). Bond trend signal is binary; a zero value is unspecified. AS suggests using it as an overlay to scale treasury exposure of other strategies. The related AS post 'Long-term returns for US Treasury funds are predictable' is a separate yield-vs-10y-return study, not this strategy.

name: SPF Recession Probability (AS reinterpretation, incl. dynamic bond)
author: Yulong Sun (AS-modified)

source.title: Navigating Economic Downturns: Insights from Survey-Based Recession Indicators

plain_english: Every quarter, checks whether professional forecasters have become more or less worried about a recession than last quarter for the same future quarters. If less worried it holds 60% stocks, otherwise it moves out of stocks; a similar check on expected 10-year yields decides whether the safe part sits in Treasuries or cash.
rules: Assume the SPF for quarter q is available by the end of the 2nd month of q (Q1 by end-Feb, Q2 by end-May, Q3 by end-Aug, Q4 by end-Nov).
At the close of the last trading day of months 2, 5, 8, 11 compute RISK_ON and BOND_ON from the latest and previous surveys.
Defensive sleeve = IEF if BOND_ON else cash (13-week T-bill).
If RISK_ON: 60% SPY + 40% defensive sleeve; else 100% defensive sleeve.
Keep the signal for the quarter; rebalance to the target mix at every month-end close.
notes: This is AS's reinterpretation, not Sun's original: Sun's first version compared RECESS2 vs lagged RECESS3; the revised paper uses RECESS4 vs lagged RECESS5, which AS considers likely overfit; Sun had no rule to exit long-duration bonds. AS averaged horizons 1-3 quarters ahead and added the TBOND rule (its own idea); the AS correlation table labels it 'SPF Recession Probability [Dynamic Bond]'. AS tightened execution to end of month 2 of the quarter. Real-world caveat: SPF release dates vary (Philadelphia Fed page lists the Q1-2026 release in March), so a live implementation should use actual release dates to avoid look-ahead. The 'anxious index' is the RECESS2 field. Sun's paper not accessed (SSRN 403).

name: Composite Strategy
author: Movement Capital (movement.capital now redirects to eversightwealth.com)

source.title: Movement Capital strategy page (Composite Strategy)

plain_english: Half of the portfolio is a permanent 50/50 mix of US/international stocks and Treasuries/TIPS. The other half is tactical: one quarter follows stock momentum versus T-bills, and one quarter holds stocks unless at least two of three US economic indicators point to recession, in which case it moves to Treasuries.
rules: At the month-end close compute MOM for SPY, EFA and SHV.
Trend-following sleeve (25%): winner = SPY or EFA with the higher MOM. If MOM_winner > MOM_SHV allocate 25% to the winner, else 25% to IEF.

Macroeconomic sleeve (25%): evaluate the three recession indicators using the prior month's (1-month lagged) economic data. If fewer than 2 indicators signal recession allocate 12.5% SPY + 12.5% EFA, otherwise 25% IEF.
Passive stock sleeve (25%): 12.5% SPY + 12.5% EFA, always.
Passive bond sleeve (25%): 12.5% IEF + 12.5% TIP, always (before 1973 the TIP half is held in IEF).
Sum sleeve weights by ticker, trade at the same close, hold to next month-end; rebalance everything to target monthly even if signals are unchanged.
notes: Simplified AS version agreed with the author. Original: Vanguard funds (VTI, VXUS, VGIT, VTIP), weekly rebalancing with a 30-day position freeze after trades (wash-sale avoidance) and exposures scaled to each client's horizon/risk tolerance; AS uses monthly month-end rebalancing. AS states the macro sleeve uses the same three indicators as Growth-Trend Timing; the exact per-indicator recession tests above are inferred from AS's GTT posts (RRSFS/INDPRO YoY<0, UNRATE above its 12-month average) and are not confirmed by Movement Capital's own page (now offline/redirected). Since May 2023 AS uses vintage economic data for this strategy (3.3% of historical months changed). Tie handling in the SPY/EFA comparison unspecified. Family is a composite (25% dual momentum, 25% macro, 50% static).

name: Active Combined Asset (ACA) - Monthly
author: Dick Stoken (month-end conversion by AllocateSmartly)

source.title: Survival of the Fittest for Investors: Using Darwin's Laws of Evolution to Build a Winning Portfolio (book)

plain_english: A once-a-month version of Stoken's three-slice breakout strategy: each slice owns stocks, gold or real estate after a 6- or 12-month high and switches to Treasuries after a 6- or 12-month low.
rules: Three 1/3 slices: SPY vs IEF, GLD vs TLT, VNQ vs IEF; start with all slices in their risk asset.

At each month-end close, a slice in defense switches to its risk asset if the risk asset's month-end close exceeds its upper channel; a slice in risk switches to defense if the close is below its lower channel; otherwise unchanged.
Trades execute at the month-end close; on any change, and at the last trading day of the calendar year, rebalance the whole portfolio to 1/3 per slice.
notes: AS replaced the 252/126 trading-day lookbacks with 12/6 month-end lookbacks and otherwise kept all rules (AS post 'Extended Backtest' section; member announcement 07/2017 says AS tracks it as a separate strategy). AS lists 'Stoken's ACA - Monthly' separately in its strategy-asset matrix and transaction-cost table. Whether the channel excludes the current month-end is inferred from the daily definition ('excluding today'). A '[Dynamic Bond]' variant also exists on AS. Lab implementation: Slices are reset to 1/3 every month (the original only rebalances on a signal change or at year-end).

name: Efficiente Index
author: J.P. Morgan

source.title: J.P. Morgan Efficiente Index methodology (index brochure/rulebook linked by AS; link now returns 404)

plain_english: Every month, a portfolio optimiser picks the mix of 12 asset-class ETFs and cash that would have earned the most over the last six months while keeping volatility under 10%, subject to caps on each asset and each asset group. Because it uses such a short window, it behaves like a momentum strategy that also rewards low volatility and low correlation.
rules: At each month-end close collect 126 trading days of daily total returns for the 12 ETFs plus cash (T-bill).
Solve the long-only, unlevered mean-variance problem: maximise expected return subject to annualised realised portfolio volatility <= 10% and the caps below.

Asset caps: SPY 20%, IWM 10%, EFA 20% (group US/developed equities <= 50%); TLT 20%, LQD 20%, HYG 20% (group US bonds <= 50%); EEM 20%, EMB 20% (group emerging markets <= 25%); VNQ 20%, DBC 10%, GLD 10% (group real assets <= 25%); TIP 50%, cash 50% (group TIPS + cash <= 50%).
AS deviation: drop any weight below 2% and redistribute it proportionally across the remaining holdings (AS ignores the original rule that weights are integer multiples of 5%).
Trade at the same close and hold until the next month-end.
notes: Constraint table transcribed from the AS post image (20180130.04.png). AS says published versions of the index differ slightly and the description is light on detail; AS 'captured the best mix'. Not specified by AS: the exact expected-return estimator, the covariance estimator, and what happens if no portfolio meets the 10% volatility cap (possible because cash is capped at 50%); JPM index documents reportedly handle infeasibility by raising the vol target stepwise - unverified here. The JPM PDF linked by AS now returns 404; the rulebook could not be retrieved. JPM's own ETF-based versions (e.g. the one behind ETF EFFE) may use different ETFs and a different vol target (unverified). Goldman Sachs' Momentum Builder Multi-Asset index is described by AS as nearly identical.

name: Defense First
author: Thomas Carlson

source.title: Defense First: A Multi-Asset Tactical Model for Adaptive Downside Protection

plain_english: The strategy ranks four defensive assets (long Treasuries, gold, commodities, US dollar) by recent momentum and gives them 40/30/20/10% of the portfolio. Any defensive asset that is doing worse than T-bills hands its share to US stocks, so stocks are owned mainly when defensive assets are weak.
rules: At the month-end close compute MOM for TLT, GLD, PDBC, UUP and BIL.
Rank the four defensive assets by MOM from highest to lowest and assign slot weights 40%, 30%, 20%, 10% by rank.
For each slot: if the asset's MOM < MOM_BIL, give that slot's weight to SPY instead; otherwise hold the asset at the slot weight.
SPY weight = sum of all redirected slots (0%-100%); SPY's own momentum is not checked.
Trade at the same close; hold until the next month-end; rebalance monthly even if unchanged.
notes: Rules from AS; the SSRN paper returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked directly. Ties in ranking and the case MOM == MOM_BIL are not addressed (AS wording 'less than' implies equality keeps the defensive asset). AS suggests (but did not implement) holding cash instead of UUP because UUP contributed almost nothing after costs, and considering a cap on stock exposure when stock momentum is negative; neither is part of the tracked rules. AS reports that results were benchmark-like after ~1980 with lower drawdowns and low correlation to other TAA strategies.

name: Hybrid Asset Allocation 60/40
author: NLX Finance (variant of Keller & Keuning's HAA-Simple)

source.title: NLX Finance HAA 60/40 variant (original publication not located); base strategy: Keller & Keuning, 'Dual and Canary Momentum with Rising Yields/Inflation: Hybrid Asset Allocation (HAA)'

plain_english: When both TIPS and US stocks have positive average momentum, hold a 60/40 mix of stocks and intermediate Treasuries; otherwise hold intermediate Treasuries if they beat T-bills, or cash if not. It is a calmer version of Keller's HAA-Simple, which holds 100% stocks when risk is on.
rules: At the month-end close compute MOM for TIP and SPY.
If MOM_TIP > 0 and MOM_SPY > 0 (risk on): hold 60% SPY + 40% IEF.
Otherwise (either is negative): if MOM_IEF > MOM_BIL hold 100% IEF, else 100% cash.
Trade at the same close; hold to next month-end; rebalance to target weights monthly.
notes: AS gives no rules beyond 'identical to HAA-Simple except 60% SPY / 40% IEF when risk on'; the full rule set above is taken from AS's HAA-Simple post. NLX Finance's own publication could not be located (no link in the AS post; nlxfinance.com does not resolve; web search unavailable). The treatment of exactly-zero momentum is unspecified. AS ran an adversarial test replacing TIPS with IEF before the TIP ETF; results were in line with the original test.

name: Dividend & Growth Allocation (DGA)
author: Paul Choi

source.title: Balance Between Growth and Dividend: Dividend & Growth Allocation

plain_english: The strategy is fully invested in either Nasdaq-100 or high-dividend US stocks, whichever has stronger momentum, but only when TIPS are in an uptrend, the S&P 500 dividend yield is at least 1.6%, and the yield curve has not been deeply inverted 7-15 months earlier. Otherwise it holds the strongest of T-bills, long Treasuries and commodities, or cash if none is trending up.
rules: At the month-end close evaluate C1, C2 and C3; risk on only if all three pass.
Risk on: compute MOM (average of 1, 3, 6, 9, 12-month % returns) for QQQ and SCHD; hold 100% of the higher one.
Risk off: compute MOM = close / 6-month SMA of month-end closes - 1 for BIL, TLT and PDBC; if the highest MOM is positive hold 100% of that asset, otherwise hold cash.
Any allocation to BIL is held as cash (AS convention).
Trade at the same close; hold until the last trading day of the next month.
notes: AS revised its post on 01/10/24 after the author revised the paper on SSRN (01/03/24) to define inversion as the 10y yield at least 0.5% below the 3m yield. AS found the yield-curve rule fragile: FRED's T10Y3MM methodology changed in June 2019, so AS self-computes the spread before that date and uses T10Y3MM afterwards. AS's monthly TIP SMA presumably uses month-end closes (price vs adjusted not stated). AS criticises the fixed 1.6% dividend-yield threshold as fit to post-1990s history and shows an adversarial version (IEF instead of simulated TIPS pre-ETF, no dividend-yield check, from 1970). Tie handling unspecified. SSRN page returned 403, so the paper was not checked directly. Lab implementation: S&P 500 dividend yield is derived from Norgate's S&P 500 total-return vs price index (trailing 12 months), lagged one month.

name: Paired Switching Strategy
author: Lewis Glenn (per AllocateSmartly); the paired-switching concept was published by A. Maewal & J. R. Bock (2011) - relationship unverified

source.title: Paired-Switching for Tactical Portfolio Allocation (Maewal & Bock, SSRN working paper) - attribution of AS's 'Glenn' version unverified

plain_english: Always fully invested in either US stocks or long-term Treasuries, whichever has performed better recently. Because the two usually move in opposite directions, the switch tends to catch whichever is in favour.
rules: At each rebalance date compute the trailing (3-month, uncertain) total return of SPY and TLT.
Hold 100% of whichever has the higher return (ties unspecified); never cash.
Hold until the next rebalance date.
notes: No dedicated public AS post. Confirmed from AS public material: the pair is SPY and TLT (AS 2019 strategy-asset matrix), the strategy uses only relative momentum with no absolute filter (AS 'Dynamic Bond' post, 11/2023), and its trading-cost drag was 0.65%/yr (2019). The lookback (3 months / prior quarter) and quarterly switching come from recollection of the Maewal & Bock paper and could not be verified (SSRN returned 403; web search quota exhausted). Inference: 0.65%/yr at 0.1% per trade implies about 3.25 full switches per year, which would require switching in ~80% of quarters under strict quarterly rebalancing; that is more consistent with a monthly check of a multi-month lookback, so AS's implementation frequency is genuinely uncertain. AS also lists Lewis Glenn as author of Quint Switching Filtered (SSRN 3129098), so 'Glenn' may be a later author of the paired-switching approach rather than the 2011 authors.

name: Quint Switching Filtered (QSF)
author: Lewis Glenn

source.title: Quint Switching Filtered (Lewis Glenn, SSRN working paper; exact title not verified)

plain_english: Look at five markets (US large caps, Nasdaq-100, developed international, emerging markets and long Treasuries). Only if all five have risen over the past three months, buy the strongest one; otherwise sit entirely in intermediate Treasuries, which happens about three months out of four.
rules: At the month-end close compute 3-month total return for SPY, QQQ, EFA, EEM and TLT.
If any of the five has R3 < 0: hold 100% IEF.
If all five have R3 > 0: hold 100% of the asset with the highest R3 (ties unspecified; exactly-zero returns unspecified).
Trade at the same close; hold until the last trading day of the next month.
notes: Rules from AS; the SSRN paper (abstract 3129098) returned 403 and was not checked directly. 'Filtered' refers to the all-positive requirement; an unfiltered 'Quint Switching' presumably holds the top 3-month performer of the five unconditionally (inferred from the name, unverified). The requested link to Scott's Investments' 'Quint Switching' could not be checked (scottsinvestments.com is now a parked domain; web search unavailable). AS notes TLT acts mainly as a spoiler (held ~2.4% of months), very high exposure to rising rates and extreme timing luck (alternate trading days CAGR 8.5%-14.8%). AS also tracks a '[Dynamic Bond]' variant (from 11/2023) that applies the momentum rule to IEF and goes to cash if it fails (presumably IEF R3 > 0 - exact form not published).

name: Momentum Based Balancing
author: Mark Virag

source.title: Momentum Based Balancing for the Diversified Portfolio (NAAIM Wagner Award paper)

plain_english: Each month the strategy looks at how nine stock, real-estate and bond ETFs plus cash did over the last three months. It shifts every return up so the second-worst asset sits at zero, drops the worst, and then allocates money in proportion to each asset's shifted return, so recent winners get the biggest slices.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of month t, compute the 3-month total return of SPY, IWM, XLB, EFA, EEM, VNQ, IEF, TLT, TIP; assign cash a 3-month return of exactly 0.
Sort the 10 values and take the second-lowest value as baseline B (B is usually negative).
For every asset (including cash) compute S_i = R3_i - B; any S_i below zero (i.e. the single lowest asset) is set to 0. The second-lowest asset therefore also ends with 0.
Sum all S_i; weight of each asset (including cash) = S_i / sum S.
Edge case not specified by AS: if sum S = 0 (all 10 returns identical) allocate 100% to cash (implementer choice). Ties at the bottom simply produce several zero weights.
Execute all trades at the same close; hold until the last trading day of the next month, then recompute and rebalance to new weights (full monthly rebalance even if ranks unchanged).
Cash portion earns the 3-month T-bill rate (AS 'cash' convention), even though its signal return is fixed at 0.
notes: AS backtest from 1973. AS describes the paper as a 2014 NAAIM Wagner Award winner; the NAAIM award page lists different 2014 top-3 winners, so the award status could not be confirmed and the paper itself was not retrieved (rules here come from AS's post, which gives a worked numeric example that matches the formula above). Price vs total return for the 3-month return is not stated explicitly; AS generally uses dividend-adjusted data with a 2-day dividend lag. Because rank-proportional weighting concentrates in whichever group (risk-on or bonds) is leading, AS also showed an Optimum-3-style variant, but that is not the tracked version.

name: Annual Seasonality
author: Fred Piard

source.title: Quantitative Investing: Strategies to Exploit Stock Market Anomalies for All Investors (Harriman House)

plain_english: Half the portfolio holds Singapore and Brazil stocks only from November to April; the other half holds German stocks only in October-December and March-April. Whenever a sleeve is out of the market it sits in cash.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of each month, determine the next calendar month m.
Sleeve A (50%): if m is November through April, hold 25% EWS and 25% EWZ; otherwise that 50% is in cash.
Sleeve B (50%): if m is October, November, December, March or April, hold 50% EWG; otherwise that 50% is in cash.
Resulting monthly targets: Jan/Feb 25 EWS/25 EWZ/50 cash; Mar/Apr 25 EWS/25 EWZ/50 EWG; May-Sep 100 cash; Oct 50 EWG/50 cash; Nov/Dec 25 EWS/25 EWZ/50 EWG.
Rebalance to these targets at every month-end close.
Before 1988 (no Brazil data in AS) allocate the full 50% of sleeve A to EWS.
notes: AS backtest from 1970. AS combined two separate Piard strategies 50/50 into one tracked strategy. AS shifted execution from Piard's next-month open to the prior month-end close. Piard's book cites classic multi-century annual-seasonality papers (not identified by name in AS text); book not checked directly. Author tickers assumed to match AS (AS does not mention any substitution).

name: Sell in May / Halloween Indicator
author: N/A (classic anomaly; academic reference Bouman & Jacobsen)

source.title: The Halloween Indicator, 'Sell in May and Go Away': Another Puzzle (Bouman & Jacobsen, American Economic Review 92(5))

plain_english: Own the S&P 500 only during the six 'winter' months from November through April and sit in cash from May through October.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of October, go 100% SPY.
Hold through November-April.
At the close of the last trading day of April, sell and go 100% cash (3-month T-bill rate).
Hold cash through May-October; repeat annually.
notes: AS backtest from 1970. AS notes many variants with different switch dates; AS uses simple month-end switching. AS lists author as N/A; the academic citation is supplied here for context only (paper itself not read beyond its listing).

name: All-Weather/All-Seasons Portfolio
author: Ray Dalio (as published by Tony Robbins)

source.title: MONEY Master the Game (Tony Robbins, interview with Ray Dalio; 'All Seasons' portfolio)

plain_english: A fixed mix designed to hold up in growth, recession, inflation and deflation: 30% US stocks, 55% Treasuries (mostly long-term), and 15% split between gold and commodities, rebalanced once a year.
rules: Hold 30% SPY, 40% TLT, 15% IEF, 7.5% GLD, 7.5% DBC at all times.
Let weights drift; once a year reset to target weights at the close (AS: annual rebalance).
No signals or trades other than the annual rebalance.
notes: No dedicated AS post. AS (Golden Butterfly post, 2016) says it tracks the version published in Robbins' 'Money: Master the Game' and assumes annual rebalancing; AS's 2019 strategy-asset matrix confirms the ETF set SPY, TLT, IEF, GLD, DBC. Weights 30/40/15/7.5/7.5 are the widely reported Robbins version (not printed in AS public text); PortfolioCharts' 'All Seasons' rounds gold/commodities to 8/7. Whether AS still rebalances annually (vs monthly) today and on which date is not verified.

name: Permanent Portfolio
author: Harry Browne

source.title: Fail-Safe Investing: Lifelong Financial Security in 30 Minutes (concept dates to Browne's early-1980s writings)

plain_english: Splits money equally four ways: US stocks for prosperity, long-term Treasuries for deflation, gold for inflation and cash for recession, then rebalances once a year.
rules: Hold 25% SPY, 25% TLT, 25% GLD, 25% cash.
Rebalance to equal 25% weights once a year at the close.
Cash earns the 3-month T-bill rate (AS tracks the cash version, not SHY).
notes: No dedicated AS post. AS Golden Butterfly post states the tracked Permanent Portfolio uses cash as the short-duration sleeve and annual rebalancing; AS 2019 strategy-asset matrix lists GLD, SPY, TLT, Cash. Browne's original band-rebalancing rule differs from AS's annual schedule (from memory; not verified here).

name: Golden Butterfly
author: Tyler (PortfolioCharts.com)

source.title: Golden Butterfly Portfolio (PortfolioCharts.com)

plain_english: Five equal 20% slices: US large stocks, US small value stocks, long-term Treasuries, short-term Treasuries and gold. It leans toward growth by doubling the stock exposure versus the Permanent Portfolio and is rebalanced once a year.
rules: Hold 20% each of SPY, IWN (US small cap value; VBR from 2025), TLT, SHY, GLD.
Rebalance to equal 20% weights once a year at the close.
AS uses SHY (not cash) for the short-term Treasury sleeve, as the author intended.
notes: PortfolioCharts page confirms the five 20% sleeves (large cap blend, small cap value, long-term Treasuries, short-term Treasuries, gold) but does not state a rebalance rule; annual rebalancing is AS's assumption. AS backtest from 1970.

name: Countercyclical Trend Following
author: Undisclosed (AS withheld the authors' names)

source.title: Undisclosed paper (title withheld by AS; AS could not confirm rules with the authors)

plain_english: Uses credit spreads and the yield curve to decide whether the economy looks stressed, inflationary or slowing, buying more risk when spreads are wide (a contrarian view). Stock and gold positions are also protected by a 200-day trend filter that moves them into Treasuries during downtrends.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of each month, take the HY spread and the 10y-1y slope as of 2 trading days earlier and compare each to its median over the trailing 10 years.
If HY spread > its 10-year median: regime = Growth (contrarian; ignore the slope). Portfolio: 50% SPY, 40% IWN, 10% GLD.
Else if slope < its 10-year median: regime = Inflation. Portfolio: 50% SPY, 10% IWN, 40% GLD.
Else (HY spread below median and slope above median): regime = Slowdown. Portfolio: 50% LQD, 40% IEF, 10% IWN.
Rebalance to the regime portfolio at that close; the regime holds until the next month-end close.
Trend overlay, maintained every day regardless of regime: an asset's state flips to downtrend after 5 consecutive closes below its 200-day SMA and to uptrend after 5 consecutive closes above it.

Whenever SPY or GLD is in downtrend, its portfolio sleeve is held in IEF instead; when it returns to uptrend the sleeve moves back. These switches are executed at the close on the day the trend state changes, including mid-month.
Pre-1990, replace IWN with IWM (US small caps) per AS.
notes: AS stated it could not confirm the exact rules with the authors and captured 'the spirit' of the strategy; original paper unidentified. Not specified: whether the 10-year medians use daily or month-end observations (uncertain), tie handling at the median, and whether the regime portfolio drifts intra-month (assume no rebalance except on trend switches). AS chose monthly regime updates (daily updating was worse after costs). Authors likely used Ken French small-value data, which AS considers unrealistically strong. AS's historical-proxy indices for GLD/LQD/IEF before ETF inception are not listed in the post (AS normally uses underlying indices). Lab implementation: Credit spread = Moody's Baa yield minus the 10-year Treasury throughout (FRED's high-yield OAS history is no longer public); macro data read at the month-end close rather than 2 days earlier; the daily trend overlay is applied at month-ends only.

name: Trending Fast and Slow (volatility-switched momentum)
author: Authors of 'Trending Fast and Slow' (Journal of Portfolio Management, 2022) - names not verified

source.title: Trending Fast and Slow (The Journal of Portfolio Management 48(3), p.103)

plain_english: Looks at how volatile the stock market was over the past month. In calm markets it follows the 12-month trend; in turbulent markets (above 17% annualized volatility) it follows only the last month's move, and it is either fully in stocks or in cash.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month compute the annualized 21-day volatility of the S&P 500 price index.
If volatility >= 17%, use the 1-month price change; otherwise use the 12-month price change.
If that change is positive, hold 100% SPY at the close; otherwise hold cash.
Hold until the last trading day of the following month.
notes: Paper not accessible (paywall/redirect) and authors could not be confirmed. AS's volatility definition (21-day log-return stdev x sqrt 252) is AS's own choice since the authors did not specify it; AS matched the authors' results closely. The 17% cutoff came from the authors' decision-tree analysis (~top quintile of observations). Original is long/short; AS long/cash. AS does not plan to track it.

name: Buy Global Stocks at All-Time Highs (else bonds)
author: Jake Moore (EconomPic) and Meb Faber

source.title: Is Buying Stocks at an All-Time High a Good Idea?

plain_english: Owns global stocks only in months when they have just closed at a record high; the rest of the time it owns US bonds. It holds stocks less than 30% of the time.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month, check whether ACWI's month-end close is a new all-time high versus all previous month-end closes.
If yes, hold 100% ACWI from that close; otherwise hold 100% AGG.
Hold until the last trading day of the following month.
notes: Faber's post describes the rule generically (stocks at all-time high -> stocks next month, else government bonds); AS chose ACWI and AGG. Whether the all-time high is measured on price or total return is not stated (AS normally uses dividend-adjusted data; uncertain). Tie (equal to prior high) treated as a high here - not specified. AS used this as an illustration that new highs are not a reason to avoid stocks; results depend heavily on bond returns.

name: 12-Month Momentum with Distance-to-1-Year-High Filter
author: Allocate Smartly

source.title: A Key New Momentum Measure to Consider: Distance from 1-Year High

plain_english: A classic rule that owns stocks when they are up over the past year, with an extra check: the market must also be in the top quarter of its 1-year price range. If it has risen over the year but fallen well off its high, it waits in cash.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month compute the S&P 500's 12-month dividend-adjusted price change.
Compute D, the position of the current close within the range of the last 13 month-end closes (0 = 1-year low, 1 = 1-year high).
If the 12-month change is positive and D >= 0.75, hold 100% SPY; otherwise hold T-bills.
Hold until the next month-end.
notes: AS's own proof of concept (no transaction costs), inspired by Alpha Architect's coverage of an SSRN paper (abstract 2900073, title not verified) on distance from the 52-week high and momentum crashes; AS changed it to a long-only, monthly, no-skip-month index strategy. Boundary (>= vs > 0.75) not stated; AS's bucket table groups 75% with the stronger bucket. Whether D uses the same dividend-adjusted series is not stated (presumed). Revised strategy reduced drawdowns but underperformed the baseline for ~20 years from the early 1990s.

name: Utilities Beta Rotation (utilities vs market relative strength)
author: Charles Bilello and Michael Gayed (identification ours; AS withheld the paper title)

source.title: An Intermarket Approach to Beta Rotation: The Strategy, Signal and Power of Utilities (2014 Charles H. Dow Award; identification not confirmed by AS)

plain_english: Each week it owns utility stocks if they have outperformed the overall market over the past four weeks (a sign of defensive positioning), otherwise it owns the whole market.
rules: At the close of each week compute the 4-week return of utilities (XLU) and of the total market (VTI).
If utilities' 4-week return is greater, hold 100% XLU for the next week; otherwise hold 100% VTI.
Repeat weekly.
notes: AS used this as a cautionary example: strong on Ken French data from 1926 but roughly market-like on tradeable index/ETF data since 1989, and would underperform after costs. AS test excluded transaction costs. Paper identity inferred from AS's description (Dow Award winner, 4-week utilities vs market) - not confirmed; source URL not retrieved. Lab implementation: Monthly approximation of the weekly rule: compares the last month's returns at month-end.

name: Commodity Momentum/Reversal with Intra-Market Correlation
author: Margareta Pauchlyova (Quantpedia)

source.title: How to Improve Commodity Momentum Using Intra-Market Correlation

plain_english: A long/short commodity sector strategy that follows momentum when the four sectors are moving together more than usual and bets on reversal when they are moving apart.
rules: At each month-end compute the 12-month return of each of the four ETFs and the short- and long-window average correlations.
If C_S > C_L (momentum regime): long the 2 ETFs with the highest 12-month return and short the 2 with the lowest.
If C_S < C_L (reversal regime, per Quantpedia): long the 2 ETFs with the lowest 12-month return and short the 2 with the highest.
Equal weights (assume +/-25% each, 100% gross - uncertain); hold for one month.
notes: AS's wording of the reversal branch appears garbled (it repeats the momentum positions); Quantpedia's article states the reversal regime goes long the 2 worst and short the 2 best, which is used here. Tie (C_S = C_L) unspecified. AS found it worked only over the author's original sample and failed in earlier years; no costs included. Long/short only. Lab implementation: Long/short at +/-25% per ETF with the remaining capital in T-bills.

name: Front-Running Commodity Seasonality (with correlation filter)
author: Cyril Dujava (Quantpedia)

source.title: Trader's Guide to Front-Running Commodity Seasonality

plain_english: Bets that commodity seasonal patterns get traded a month early: each month it goes long or short four commodity sector funds depending on whether their return in the corresponding month a year earlier was strong or weak. A filter moves to cash when the four commodities start moving too much in lockstep.
rules: At each month-end, for each ETF take its return in the month 11 months before the month being positioned for (e.g. at end-December use the previous February).
Rank that return against the ETF's own monthly returns since then; at or above the median -> long, below -> short.
Base version: +/-25% of capital in each ETF (net exposure between -100% and +100%).
Risk-parity variant: size each position inversely to its trailing 36-month volatility (scaling to 100% gross assumed - uncertain).
Correlation-filter variant: if the 20-day average pairwise correlation exceeds the 250-day average, hold 100% cash for the month.
Long-only variant (AS Test #3, includes the correlation filter): short signals become cash (each ETF slot 25%).
Hold all positions until the next month-end.
notes: AS post lists 'DBC: Energy' - a typo for DBE (later text says DBE). Proof of concept: AS ignored transaction and shorting costs. AS found results concentrated in 2000-2010 and flat otherwise; the correlation filter improved Sharpe. Quantpedia's article gives the 20/250-day windows only in its companion momentum article; exact averaging formula (pairwise mean) not stated - uncertain. Risk-parity sizing formula not stated by AS. Long-short base is the author's design; the long-only variant is AS's. Lab implementation: Long-only version with the correlation filter (AllocateSmartly's test #3); percentile uses the last 12 monthly returns.

name: Front-Running Seasonality in Country ETFs
author: Sona Beluska (Quantpedia)

source.title: Front Running in Country ETFs, or How to Spot and Leverage Seasonality

plain_english: Assumes investors anticipate each country's seasonal pattern a month early. Each month it buys the 8 country funds that did best, a year ago, in the month that is now one month ahead, with larger weights for the top ranks.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of month t, rank all available country ETFs by their return in month t-10.
Select the top 8 and weight them: ranks 1-3 18.18% each, rank 4 15.15%, rank 5 12.12%, rank 6 9.09%, rank 7 6.06%, rank 8 3.03% (i.e. 6,6,6,5,4,3,2,1 /33).
Hold until the last trading day of the following month and repeat.
ETFs enter the universe only once data exist (Quantpedia added EZA, FXI, INDY after their launches).
notes: Quantpedia's final portfolio averages six sub-portfolios (top 3, 4, ..., 8); AS translated this into the rank weights above (AS assumption, matched their overlap closely). If each sub-portfolio were equal-weighted internally, weights would be the 'alt' set (our computation). AS results exclude transaction costs and AS declined to track (not consistently effective since 1971, esp. late 1990s). Without the front-running month (same month last year) results were worse.

name: Max Diversification Portfolio (US Max Diversification)
author: AllocateSmartly (N/A developer); technique from Choueifaty & Coignard

source.title: Testing Popular Portfolio Optimization Techniques (AllocateSmartly)

plain_english: Holds US stocks, Treasuries, corporate bonds and REITs in the mix that maximises diversification - the ratio of the assets' average stand-alone volatility to the portfolio's actual volatility - using the last three years of monthly data.
rules: At the month-end close compute monthly returns from the last 36 month-end dividend-adjusted closes for SPY, IEF, LQD, VNQ.
Maximise DR(w) subject to w_i >= 0 and sum(w) = 1 (no min/max per asset, no cash, no leverage). Equivalent QP: minimise y' Sigma y s.t. sigma' y = 1, y >= 0; then w = y / sum(y).
Trade at the close; hold until next month-end.
notes: AS tracks this as a generic, unoptimised benchmark-like strategy on the four largest US asset classes. Whether '36 month-end values' means 36 returns (37 prices) or 35 returns is ambiguous. AS observed it tends to ignore LQD. AS's 2019 matrix and later posts label it 'US Max Diversification'; a global extension was mentioned but not found.

name: Equal Risk Contribution Portfolio (US Equal Risk Contribution)
author: AllocateSmartly (N/A developer); technique from Maillard, Roncalli & Teiletche

source.title: Testing Popular Portfolio Optimization Techniques (AllocateSmartly)

plain_english: Splits money across US stocks, Treasuries, corporate bonds and REITs so that each contributes the same amount of risk to the portfolio, accounting for both volatility and correlation, re-estimated monthly from three years of data.
rules: At the month-end close estimate Sigma from the last 36 month-end dividend-adjusted closes of SPY, IEF, LQD, VNQ.
Find w with w_i >= 0, sum(w) = 1 such that RC_i is equal for all assets (true ERC using full covariance, not 1/vol).
Trade at the close; hold until next month-end.
notes: AS stresses this is true ERC (covariance-based) rather than naive inverse-volatility. AS also uses ERC as an alternative benchmark and as half of the Meta Strategy weighting (with Min Correlation) - those are different applications. 36-value ambiguity as in Max Diversification.

name: Max Sharpe Portfolio (US Max Sharpe)
author: AllocateSmartly (N/A developer); inspired by Keller, Butler & Kipnis 'Momentum and Markowitz: A Golden Combination'

source.title: Testing Popular Portfolio Optimization Techniques (AllocateSmartly)

plain_english: Picks the mix of US stocks, Treasuries, corporate bonds and REITs with the best historical return per unit of risk, once using three years of data and once using one year, and averages the two. The one-year half makes it lean toward recent winners, giving it a momentum tilt.
rules: At the month-end close compute mu and Sigma for SPY, IEF, LQD, VNQ from the last 36 monthly returns and, separately, from the last 12 monthly returns.
Solve the long-only, fully invested tangency (max Sharpe) portfolio for each window (QP: minimise y' Sigma y s.t. (mu - rf)' y = 1, y >= 0; w = y/sum(y)).
Average the two weight vectors 50/50.
Trade at the close; hold until next month-end.
notes: Only AS's own description is available. Not stated: expected-return estimator, risk-free rate, behaviour when no asset has excess return > 0 (fallback unknown). Higher turnover and fewer positions than the other optimisers. Labelled 'US Max Sharpe' in later AS posts. | Family set to 'risk-parity' = AS 'Portfolio Optimization' bucket (mean-variance, not strictly risk parity). Lab implementation: Expected return = mean monthly return over each window; cash rate = T-bill return over the same window; if no asset beats cash, the minimum-variance portfolio is used.

name: US Min Correlation
author: AllocateSmartly (N/A developer); algorithm by David Varadi

source.title: Testing Popular Portfolio Optimization Techniques (AllocateSmartly)

plain_english: Holds US stocks, Treasuries, corporate bonds and REITs, overweighting those least correlated with the others and least volatile, based on three years of monthly data.
rules: At the month-end close compute monthly returns from the last 36 month-end closes of SPY, IEF, LQD, VNQ.
Apply the Minimum Correlation Algorithm (normalised correlation matrix, rank weights, inverse-volatility scaling) to get long-only weights summing to 100%.
Trade at the close; hold until next month-end.
notes: Extra entry (not in the assigned list): AS tracks this separately from 'Varadi's Minimum Correlation Portfolio' (it appears as 'US Min Correlation' in AS tables through 2026 and in the 2019 asset matrix with IEF/LQD/SPY/VNQ). Drop if the catalog should only contain the current list-of-strategies names.

name: Diversified Dual Momentum
author: Corey Hoffstein (Newfound Research)

source.title: Fragility Case Study: Dual Momentum GEM

plain_english: Gary Antonacci's Dual Momentum picks US stocks, international stocks, or bonds using one 12-month lookback. This version runs the same rule seven times with lookbacks from 6 to 12 months and splits the money equally, so one unlucky lookback choice matters less.
rules: At the month-end close, for each of the 7 lookbacks L = 6..12 months run Antonacci's GEM decision:
Absolute momentum: if R_SPY(L) > H(L), hold whichever of SPY and EFA has the higher R(L) (relative momentum); otherwise hold AGG.
Each of the 7 sub-portfolios is allocated 1/7 of capital; sum the sub-portfolio holdings to get final weights (multiples of 1/7 across SPY, EFA, AGG).
Trade at the close; hold until the next month-end.
notes: No dedicated public AS post; AS added it to the members area in Jan 2019 and summarised it as GEM split into 7 equal parts with lookbacks of 6-12 months. AS's 2019 asset matrix lists SPY, EFA, AGG (no cash). Newfound's text gives the 6-12 month range, 7 models, equal weighting and an annual rebalance of the blend; the GEM decision tree itself is an image. Unverified: whether AS uses calendar months or 21-day multiples, the exact T-bill hurdle series, and whether AS rebalances sleeves monthly (assumed) rather than annually. AS also tracks a 'Dynamic Bond' variant (AGG must also pass the absolute-momentum rule, else cash) - not specified here.

name: Mama Bear Portfolio
author: Brian Livingston (Muscular Portfolios)

source.title: Muscular Portfolios: The Investing Revolution for Superior Returns with Lower Risk (book) / MuscularPortfolios.com Mama Bear page

plain_english: Every month, look at nine broad asset classes (US large and small stocks, foreign and emerging stocks, real estate, commodities, gold, long Treasuries and cash), and put a third of your money into each of the three that rose most over the past five months.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month, compute the 5-month total return for each of the 9 candidates: SPY, IWM, EFA, EEM, VNQ, DBC, GLD, TLT and cash (SHV in the original; AS replaces SHV with cash).
Rank all 9 by 5-month return and select the top 3 regardless of whether their returns are positive or negative (no absolute-momentum filter).
Allocate 1/3 of the portfolio to each selected asset at the close (if cash ranks in the top 3, that 1/3 is held in cash).
Hold until the last trading day of the following month; rebalance all positions back to 1/3 each month even if holdings do not change.
Tie-breaks are not specified by the author or AS.
notes: AS mapping of author tickers to AS ETFs inferred by asset class (VONE Russell 1000 -> SPY; VIOO S&P 600 -> IWM). Livingston's website measures 105 trading days using the prior day's closes and trades any consistent day; AS uses month-end and a 5-month lookback, justified because the book backtests used Faber's Idea Farm monthly workbook. AS models SHV as cash. Livingston also suggests trading only when bid-ask spread <1%. AS notes month-end trading has historically been notably better than other days for this model. Backtest start year not given in the AS text. Near-clone of CXO's SACEMS concept.

name: Papa Bear Portfolio
author: Brian Livingston (Muscular Portfolios)

source.title: Muscular Portfolios: The Investing Revolution for Superior Returns with Lower Risk (book) / MuscularPortfolios.com Papa Bear page

plain_english: Every month, score 13 asset classes (US growth and value stocks large and small, foreign and emerging stocks, real estate, commodities, gold, several kinds of bonds) by their average 3-, 6- and 12-month gains, and split the money equally among the top three. It never goes to cash.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month, compute SCORE = average of the 3-, 6- and 12-month total returns for each of the 13 ETFs.
Select the 3 ETFs with the highest SCORE regardless of sign (no absolute-momentum filter, no cash option).
Allocate 1/3 of the portfolio to each at the close.
Hold until the last trading day of the following month; rebalance to 1/3 each monthly even if holdings are unchanged.
Tie-breaks are not specified.
notes: Author ETF-to-AS mapping inferred by asset class (e.g., EDV extended-duration Treasuries -> TLT, VCLT long corporate -> LQD); AS end notes list the 13 AS tickers. Livingston's site uses trading-day lookbacks and allows any consistent trading day; AS uses calendar months at month-end (book results were based on Faber's monthly Idea Farm workbook). AS's Papa Bear test is shorter than Mama Bear's; exact start years not stated in text. Considered a near-clone of Faber's GTAA Agg 3 without the absolute-momentum filter.

name: Growth-Trend Timing (GTT-Original)
author: Philosophical Economics (pseudonymous blogger 'Jesse Livermore')

source.title: Growth and Trend: A Simple, Powerful Technique for Timing the Stock Market

plain_english: Stay fully in US stocks whenever both retail sales and industrial production are growing year over year. Only when one of them is shrinking (a recession warning) do you let the classic 10-month moving average decide whether to stay in stocks or move to cash.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of month m, read FRED RRSFS (Real Retail and Food Services Sales) and INDPRO (Industrial Production Index) for month m-1 (FRED date m-1/01), using the data vintage available at that date (AS uses vintage/ALFRED data since May 2023).
Compute the year-over-year change of each series for month m-1 versus month m-13.
If both YoY changes are positive: no recession signal; hold 100% SPY regardless of price trend.

If either YoY change is negative: recession signal; check trend. If SPY's month-end close is above its 10-month simple moving average of month-end closes (current month included), hold 100% SPY; otherwise hold 100% cash (3-month T-bills).
Execute at the same close; hold until the last trading day of the following month.
Alternate (non-month-end) trading days in AS use data lagged one further month (m-2).
notes: PE also tested a daily version with a 200-day MA and other growth signals (real EPS, employment, real personal income, housing starts); PE's preferred combination is retail sales + industrial production, which AS tests. PE compares the S&P 500 total-return index with its 10-month average; AS does not say whether its SMA uses price or dividend-adjusted closes (AS generally uses dividend-adjusted data). AS notes replacing cash with IEF or AGG would have raised returns ~1%/yr (not part of the rules). Vintage data changed 1.7% of historical monthly allocations. Exact behaviour at a YoY of exactly 0 is not specified. Lab implementation: Real retail sales growth = nominal retail sales growth minus CPI inflation (Norgate), a close stand-in for FRED RRSFS.

name: Growth-Trend Timing - UE Rate
author: Philosophical Economics (pseudonymous blogger 'Jesse Livermore')

source.title: In Search of the Perfect Recession Indicator

plain_english: Stay fully in US stocks unless last month's unemployment rate has climbed above its own 12-month average, which tends to happen near recessions. In that case, hold stocks only if the market is above its 10-month moving average; otherwise sit in cash.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of month m, take FRED UNRATE (civilian unemployment rate, seasonally adjusted) for months m-12 through m-1, using the vintage available at that date (AS uses ALFRED vintages since May 2023: all 12 values as known at month-end m, including any revisions released by then but none after).
Compute the 12-month average of UNRATE over months m-12..m-1.
If UNRATE for month m-1 is higher than that 12-month average: recession signal; otherwise no recession signal.
No recession signal: hold 100% SPY regardless of price.
Recession signal: hold 100% SPY if SPY's month-end close is above its 10-month SMA of month-end closes (current month included); otherwise hold 100% cash (3-month T-bills).
Execute at the same close; hold until the last trading day of the following month. AS alternate (earlier) trading days use data lagged one extra month.
notes: PE's original UE post compares the unemployment rate to its trailing 12-month MA and the S&P 500 total-return index to its 10-month MA; PE does not discuss publication lag, AS adds a 1-month lag. AS's 2019 redux tests both GTT variants from 1930 and says they agree ~96% of the time. Vintage data changed 0.9% of historical monthly allocations. AS does not state whether its SPY SMA uses price or dividend-adjusted closes. Equality (UE exactly equal to SMA) treated as no recession per AS wording 'higher than'. This rule is also the timing engine in Keller's Lethargic Asset Allocation and is closely related to Novell's SPY-UI/Bond UI1.

name: Bond UI1
author: Paul Novell (Investing for a Living)

source.title: Enhancing Returns of TAA Bond Strategies / Adding Zero Yield Assets to TAA Bond Strategies / Using Economic Indicators to Time the Market (UI indicator)

plain_english: A bond strategy driven only by the unemployment rate: while unemployment is falling relative to its 1-year average it holds a mix of credit-risk bonds; when unemployment turns up it switches to Treasuries, gold and cash.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of month m, compare the unemployment rate (UNRATE) for month m-1 with its 12-month simple moving average (vintage data as of that date).
If UNRATE is below (not above) its 12-month SMA: risk on - hold equal weights (25% each) of HYG, LQD, BNDX, EMB.
If UNRATE is above its 12-month SMA: risk off - hold equal weights of the government/hedge basket: IEF, TLT, GLD and cash (Novell's GOVH set is SHY, IEF, TLT, GLD; AS models SHY as cash) - uncertain.
Hold until the next month-end; rebalance to equal weights monthly.
notes: No dedicated public AS post; AS's Aug 2019 announcement says Bond UI1 uses the US unemployment rate to switch between credit-risk bonds and US government bonds/gold, and AS's vintage-data post lists it. Novell's Jul 2019 post defines UI1 as CRED (HYG, EMB, BNDX, LQD equal weight) vs GOV (SHY, IEF, TLT equal weight) switched by his simple monthly SPY-UI indicator (UNRATE vs 12-month SMA, Part 1 of his 2016 series, no price confirmation); his Aug 2019 post adds GLD (GOVH). AS's 'government bonds/gold' wording suggests the GLD version - exact AS risk-off basket and whether AS applies a trend filter are unverified. Superseded by Bond-COMP; AS flagged it as a candidate for future removal.

name: Tactical Bond Strategy
author: Paul Novell (Investing for a Living)

source.title: A Trend Following Bond Portfolio for Any Environment (GTAA Bond 3)

plain_english: Each month, pick the three bond types (from short, intermediate and long Treasuries, inflation-protected, corporate, high-yield, international and emerging-market bonds) with the best 6-month returns, and give each a third of the money - but only if it beat both zero and T-bills; otherwise that third goes to cash.
rules: At the close on the last trading day of the month, compute the 6-month total return of SHY, IEF, TLT, TIP, LQD, HYG, BNDX and EMB (assets without data at that date are excluded - implied by AS).
Rank and select the top 3 by 6-month return.
For each of the 3: if its 6-month return is positive AND greater than BIL's 6-month return, allocate 1/3 of the portfolio to it; otherwise allocate that 1/3 to cash.
Any 1/3 slot assigned to SHY is held as cash instead (AS convention).
Hold until the last trading day of the following month; rebalance the entire portfolio monthly even if holdings are unchanged. Tie-breaks unspecified.
notes: Rules are fully stated by AS (Jan 2017). AS adds the BIL hurdle (author used only a positive-return hurdle) and executes at month-end same-day close (author: every 4 weeks, next-day close). Novell's 2014 original 'GTAA Bond 3' had a different/expanded universe (JNK, IGOV, MUB, later EMB) and his 2019 update cites 9 ETFs; the AS 8-asset universe was not reconciled with Novell's current list. AS backtest from 1970 with limited data for several assets; benchmark = equal weight of live assets.

name: TrendYCMacro
author: Ďurian and Radovan Vojtko (Quantpedia)

source.title: Avoid Equity Bear Markets with a Market Timing Strategy

plain_english: Holds the US stock market or cash. It stays invested while the economy (retail sales, industrial production and housing starts) is growing year over year, and otherwise only buys stocks when price trend, a return-asymmetry trend measure, and a non-inverted yield curve all agree.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of month m, compute YoY change of RRSFS (real retail & food services sales), INDPRO (industrial production) and HOUST (housing starts) using the data point for month m-1 vs month m-13 (vintage/as-first-available data where possible).
If all three YoY changes are > 0 AND the strategy is currently long SPY, stay 100% SPY (macro strength can only maintain, never initiate, a long position).

Otherwise compute, from daily SPY returns in excess of BIL (T-bill) returns: (a) excess-return index above its 200-day simple average; (b) 200-day Rachev ratio RR(0.5,0.5) > 1; (c) 10-year Treasury yield > 3-month Treasury yield.
If (a), (b) and (c) are all true, go/stay 100% SPY at the close.
If neither the macro-persistence condition nor the full trend+yield-curve condition holds, move 100% to cash (AS: BIL-destined funds are held as cash earning 13-week T-bill return).
Hold until the close of the last trading day of the following month.
notes: AS replicated using the authors' exact calculations; AS results ~40 bp/yr lower due to 0.1%/trade costs, SPY expense ratio pre-ETF, vintage macro data and non-French data. AS backtest from 1927. Discrepancy with Quantpedia's blog series (Part 3): the blog's final TrendYCMacro uses INDPROD, RSALES and DIVIDEND (Shiller real dividends) for the macro branch, not HOUST; AS (post Sept 2023, from authors' final paper) lists RRSFS, INDPRO, HOUST - follow AS. Quantpedia Part 1 defines Trend as AND of 200-day SMA and RR(0.5,0.5)>1 on market excess returns, monthly decision. Rachev>1 with a median split is practically equivalent to the 200-day mean daily excess return being positive. Whether the 200-day SMA window includes the current day, and exact macro proxies before RRSFS (1992) / HOUST (1959), are not public. Original SSRN PDF could not be accessed (403).

name: Gold Cross-Asset Momentum
author: Cyril Dujava (Quantpedia)

source.title: Cross-Asset Price-Based Regimes for Gold

plain_english: Own gold only when both gold and intermediate Treasuries have risen over the past year; otherwise sit in cash. The idea is that gold does best when falling yields (rising bond prices) and gold's own trend agree.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of the month compute 12-month total return of GLD and IEF.
If both are strictly positive, hold 100% GLD; otherwise hold 100% cash (13-week T-bill return).
IEF is a signal only and is never held.
Hold until the close of the following month.
notes: Quantpedia sample 1969-12 to 2025-09; author tested 1/3/6/12-month windows and all four joint sign states, recommending only the 12-month GLD-up/IEF-up state. Author's cash leg earns Fed Funds; AS uses T-bills (cash). AS backtest from 1970. AS frames it as a small-allocation diversifier or a gold overlay rather than a standalone portfolio.

name: Optimal Trend Following
author: Valeriy Zakamulin and Javier Giner

source.title: Optimal Trend Following Rules in Two-State Regime-Switching Models

plain_english: A trend signal for the S&P 500 that rewards recent gains (last ~8 months) but treats gains from 10-30 months ago as a sign the bull run may be getting old. Invest when the combined score is positive, otherwise hold cash.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of each month, compute the weighted sum of the last 30 monthly total returns of the S&P 500 using the optimal weights (positive for lags 1-8, ~0 at lag 9, negative for lags 10-30).
If the indicator is positive, hold 100% SPY; otherwise hold 100% cash (13-week T-bill return).
Hold until the close of the following month.
notes: Weights are derived by the authors from a two-state semi-Markov (duration-dependent) regime-switching model calibrated to 1897-2020 US data, maximizing Sharpe ratio; no price optimisation. AS gives only the qualitative shape (bullish <=8m, bearish 10-30m) and the chart; the numbers above are a pixel read of that chart (lag 9 ~0, lag 30 still slightly negative - weights beyond lag 30 assumed zero; uncertain). Whether the authors' rule uses excess or total returns is not confirmed (AS says dividend-adjusted returns). SSRN PDF inaccessible (403); verify weights against the paper before production use.

name: US Cross-Asset Momentum
author: Aleksi Pitkäjärvi, Matti Suominen, Lauri Vaittinen

source.title: Cross-asset signals and time series momentum (Journal of Financial Economics)

plain_english: Holds US stocks when both stocks and Treasuries have beaten cash over the past year, holds Treasuries when bonds are up but stocks are down, and otherwise sits in cash. It uses the finding that rising bond prices are good news for stocks while strong stocks are bad news for bonds.
rules: At month-end compute 12-month excess returns of SPY and IEF over T-bills.
If XS_SPY > 0 and XS_IEF > 0: hold 100% SPY.
Else if XS_SPY < 0 and XS_IEF > 0: hold 100% IEF.
Otherwise (IEF excess return <= 0): hold 100% cash.
Hold until the close of the following month.
notes: AS tests a simplified long-only, unlevered, US-only version; the paper trades long/short across many international markets, combining own-asset TSMOM with cross-asset signals (bond past returns positive predictor for equities; equity past returns negative predictor for bonds). Whether excess return is the difference of compounded 12m returns or of summed monthly excess returns is not specified (immaterial for sign in most cases). Treatment of exactly-zero values not specified. Spends ~half of months in cash.

name: US Risk Parity Trend-Following
author: Andrew Clare, James Seaton, Peter N. Smith, Stephen Thomas

source.title: The Trend is Our Friend: Risk Parity, Momentum and Trend Following in Global Asset Allocation

plain_english: Gives each of five US asset classes a weight inversely proportional to its volatility, so calm assets like Treasuries get more money. Each asset is held only while it trades above its 10-month average; otherwise its share sits in cash.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of each month, compute 12-month volatility for SPY, IWM, IEF, DBC, VNQ and set inverse-volatility weights summing to 100%.
For each asset: if its close is above its 10-month SMA, hold its risk-parity weight; otherwise hold that weight in cash (13-week T-bill).
Hold until the last trading day of the following month; rebalance the whole portfolio monthly even if signals are unchanged.
notes: AS tested the broad asset-class strategy of Section 3.1 of the paper. Average cash ~30%. AS mentions it would prefer ERC (covariance-aware) to simple RP but tests simple RP. Asness et al. originally estimated vol with a 3-year window of monthly excess returns and scaled to a vol target with leverage; AS uses a 12-month window, unlevered weights summing to 100% (normalisation assumed). Data frequency of the 12-month vol is not stated. AS 2022+ commodity ETF stitch DBC->PDBC per AS conventions. Journal: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Finance (2016); SSRN version 2012. Paper PDF not accessed (SSRN 403). Lab implementation: Trend is tested on total-return prices rather than cash prices (small difference).

name: Global Risk Parity Trend-Following
author: Andrew Clare, James Seaton, Peter N. Smith, Stephen Thomas

source.title: The Trend is Our Friend: Risk Parity, Momentum and Trend Following in Global Asset Allocation

plain_english: A global version of the inverse-volatility plus 10-month trend filter idea, using US and international stocks, emerging markets, US and international government bonds, commodities and global REITs. Assets below trend are swapped for cash, keeping the portfolio balanced and low-volatility.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of each month, compute 12-month volatility for all 7 assets and inverse-volatility weights, halving the raw weight of SPY, EFA, IEF and BWX (they split one asset-class slot each: US/intl equities and US/intl government bonds), then normalise to 100%.
For each asset: if its close is above its 10-month SMA, hold its weight; otherwise that weight goes to cash (13-week T-bill).
Hold until the last trading day of the following month; rebalance the whole portfolio monthly.
notes: AS's parenthetical says 'sigma-hat is multiplied by 0.5' but the main text says these assets get half their normal risk-parity weight; implement as half weight (multiplier on 1/sigma). The half allocation also applies to AS's equal-weight benchmark. AS 2025 ticker conventions may replace EFA->IEFA, EEM->IEMG, RWO->REET and DBC->PDBC (from ~2022) - not stated in this 2017 post; verify. Normalisation to 100% and the vol return frequency are assumptions. AS notes alternate-trading-day results suggest the month-end timing may be slightly optimistic. Lab implementation: Trend is tested on total-return prices rather than cash prices (small difference).

name: Pragmatic Asset Allocation
author: Radovan Vojtko and Javorská (Quantpedia)

source.title: Pragmatic Asset Allocation Model for Semi-Active Investors

plain_english: Four overlapping sleeves each rebalance once a year, buying the two strongest of world stocks, Nasdaq-100 and emerging markets if they are in uptrends, or moving to gold/Treasuries/cash when the yield curve is inverted or trends fail. Positions are designed to be held at least a year for tax efficiency, with a quarterly trend check as a safety valve.
rules: Split the portfolio into 4 independent tranches of 25%. Tranche k trades only once per year, at the close of the last trading day of its month (1, 4, 7 or 10), using data as of the end of the previous month (12, 3, 6 or 9).
For the trading tranche: if the yield curve is inverted (10Y <= 3M at the signal date), send the whole 25% tranche to the defensive step.

Otherwise rank ACWI, QQQ, EEM by MOM12 descending. For each of the top two only: if UP_i, allocate 12.5% of the total portfolio to it; if not, that 12.5% goes to the defensive step (the 3rd-ranked asset never substitutes).

Defensive step for the amount D sent to defense: rank IEF, GLD, BIL by MOM12 descending; each of the top two receives D/2 if UP_i, otherwise its D/2 goes to cash. BIL allocations are held as cash (AS convention). A tranche can therefore hold up to 3 assets (1 risky + 2 defensive).

Stop-loss on the other three (non-trading) tranches at each tranche date (months 1,4,7,10): for every asset they hold, if the asset's prior month-end close < its SMA12 (as of prior month-end) AND it has been held more than 12 months, sell that slice to cash and keep it in cash until that tranche's next scheduled trade.
Every month-end, rebalance all holdings back to their target fraction of the whole portfolio (simplifying assumption of the authors, matched by AS).
All trades at the close of the last trading day of the month.
notes: AS also tracks a 'Pragmatic Asset Allocation - Amended' variant (seen in AS correlation table alongside '- Original'): per Quantpedia's follow-up 'A few thoughts on Pragmatic Asset Allocation', the yield-curve risk-off switch is valid for only 12 months; after that, if the curve is still inverted but the moving-average price signal is positive, the YC signal is ignored. Exact AS implementation of the amended version is not public. Unclear details: how tranches are seeded at backtest start (assume staggered start), and whether 'held more than 12 months' counts continuous holding across a tranche's re-selection (AS wording implies yes). Quantpedia says the authors' stop-loss is checked only on quarterly dates and executed at the next tranche date. AS notes 2025 ETF swaps (EEM->IEMG) may apply - verify. Authors' backtest starts 1928; AS starts 1970. Lab implementation: The four tranches are seeded with the same allocation at the start of the backtest.

name: Multi-Asset Trend Following (1, 3 and 12-month time-series momentum)
author: Brian K. Hurst, Yao Hua Ooi, Lasse H. Pedersen

source.title: A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing (Journal of Portfolio Management)

plain_english: A managed-futures style trend follower built from ETFs. It goes long assets that have beaten cash over the last 1, 3 and 12 months and short those that have lagged, across US and international stocks, REITs, Treasuries, inflation-linked and corporate bonds, gold, silver, commodities, oil and the dollar. Every asset gets the same risk budget and the whole book targets 10% volatility, so it uses leverage on quiet assets. Its value is that it tends to make money in long equity bear markets.
rules: At the close of the last trading day of each month, for each asset with at least 13 months of history, compare its 1, 3 and 12-month total return with cash over the same windows. Each window votes +1 (above cash) or -1 (below cash); the signal is the average vote, so it ranges from fully long (+1) to fully short (-1).

Size each position to the same risk: 10% annualised volatility divided by the number of assets, using an exponentially weighted volatility of daily returns (60-day half-life). Low-volatility assets such as Treasuries therefore get larger notional weights than equities or commodities.

Scale the whole book so its expected volatility, from the last 126 trading days of daily returns, is 10% a year (never more than 4x the raw weights). Cash takes the remainder: it is negative when the book is leveraged and above 100% when it is net short.
Hold for one month, then repeat.
notes: Adapted from the paper's futures universe (67 markets, 1880-2016) to 15 ETFs, with monthly instead of daily rebalancing and the lab's 0.10% trading cost; no management or performance fees, no extra borrow fee on short ETF positions, and leverage financed at the T-bill rate (a broker charges more). Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen build on Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen (2012), Time Series Momentum, Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2011.11.003. Added from a cross-asset diversifier study (Nov 2026), where a weekly version had a correlation of about -0.04 with an equity-timing portfolio and negative correlation in months when the Nasdaq-100 fell.

name: Multi-Asset Trend Following, ex-equity (bonds, credit, metals, commodities, dollar)
author: Brian K. Hurst, Yao Hua Ooi, Lasse H. Pedersen

source.title: A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing (Journal of Portfolio Management)

plain_english: The same trend follower without any stocks: it rides or shorts trends in government and corporate bonds, gold, silver, commodities, oil and the dollar, with equal risk per asset and 10% target volatility. It is designed to add returns that are unrelated to the stock market.
rules: Same rules as the multi-asset version, applied only to Treasuries, inflation-linked, corporate and high-yield bonds, gold, silver, broad commodities, oil and the US dollar.
Leaving equities out makes it a pure diversifier for a stock-heavy portfolio: its return does not depend on the equity market's direction.
notes: Ex-equity variant of hop_trend_multi_asset (same adaptations: 10 ETFs, monthly rebalancing, 0.10% trading cost, no fees, no extra borrow fee, leverage financed at the T-bill rate). Added from the same cross-asset diversifier study (Nov 2026).
